title: 19  Bias, variance, and the assumptions of the linear model
text:
19.8 Check your understanding
1. What is bias in the context of a statistical model?

 It is the difference between observed and predicted values. It is the systematic error caused by a model that is too simple to capture the real pattern in the data. A linear model fit to a curved relationship is biased. It is the same as variance. It is the error caused by having too few participants.

2. What is “variance” in the bias-variance trade-off?

 The variance of the outcome variable. The error caused by a model that is too sensitive to the specific data it was fit to: it captures noise as well as signal, so its predictions are unstable across different samples. This is also called overfitting. The variance of the predictor variable. An error that affects only inference, not estimation.

3. What is the bias-variance trade-off?

 More complex models always have less variance and less bias. More complex models always have more bias and less variance. Making a model more complex generally reduces bias (it can capture more patterns) but increases variance (it becomes more sensitive to noise). The two cannot be minimized simultaneously, and the best total fit is at some intermediate complexity. Bias and variance are unrelated to model complexity.

4. Why can plain R-squared be misleading when comparing models with different numbers of predictors?

 R-squared decreases when you add a useless predictor. R-squared increases (or stays the same) when you add a predictor, even if the predictor is random noise. This means R-squared on its own cannot tell you whether adding a predictor genuinely improved the model. Adjusted R-squared partially corrects for this by penalizing each added predictor. R-squared only changes if the new predictor is perfectly correlated with the outcome. R-squared can go negative when you add too many predictors.

5. What does the mnemonic LINE stand for?

 L = Linearity, I = Independence, N = Normality of residuals, E = Equal variance (homoscedasticity). L = Lines, I = Indicators, N = Numbers, E = Estimates. L = Least, I = Indicator, N = Noise, E = Error. Linearity, Inference, Normality, Equality.

6. Where do you look to check linearity and homoscedasticity?

 By plotting the raw outcome and checking it is bell-shaped. By plotting the residuals against the fitted values and checking for systematic patterns (a curve indicates linearity violation; a fan indicates heteroscedasticity). By computing the mean of the predictors. By looking at the t-statistic of each predictor.

7. What does the normality assumption say?

 The raw outcome should be normally distributed. The residuals (not the raw outcome) should be approximately normally distributed. You check this with a Q-Q plot: points falling on the diagonal indicate approximate normality. All variables should be normally distributed. The slope estimate should be normally distributed; this is automatically true.

8. When is the independence assumption typically violated?

 When two predictors are highly correlated. When observations are clustered or nested (e.g., students within classrooms, repeated measurements on the same person, networked data). The residuals of clustered observations are correlated with each other, and standard OLS standard errors become misleadingly small. When the outcome is categorical. When the sample size is below 30.

20.1 Overview
Chapter 19 introduced the bias-variance trade-off and the four LINE assumptions of OLS regression. This chapter takes the diagnostic side and makes it practical in R, then closes Section 3 by surveying when the linear model is not enough and where to go beyond it.
By the end of the chapter you will:
This chapter is short on new prose and long on visuals. The point is to see what each diagnostic looks like and how to act on it.

title: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model
text:
20.2 Diagnostic plots in R
You fit a model with lm(), and then you check it. R provides four diagnostic plots automatically when you call plot() on a model object. In an interactive session, R will display them one at a time; in a script you usually want to see them together:

model <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility * condition, data = data)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))   # 2x2 layout
plot(model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))   # reset

The four plots produced are:

Residuals vs Fitted. Linearity and homoscedasticity.
Normal Q-Q. Normality of residuals.
Scale-Location. Another view of homoscedasticity.
Residuals vs Leverage. Influential observations.

In what follows we walk through each one, with code you can run on your own.

20.2.1 Plot 1: Residuals vs Fitted
This plot displays the residual of each observation (vertical axis) against the model’s predicted value for that observation (horizontal axis). It is the most useful of the diagnostic plots, because two of the four LINE assumptions show up here:

Linearity: the residuals should scatter randomly around zero, with no systematic curve. A U-shape or inverted-U indicates a nonlinear relationship the model is missing.
Homoscedasticity: the spread of the residuals should be roughly constant across the range of fitted values. A fan or cone shape indicates heteroscedasticity.

On our vgames data, with an interaction model:









The red curve is a smooth trend through the residuals. A nearly flat red curve at zero, like above, is what you want. A clear curve in the red line would indicate a linearity problem.


20.2.2 Plot 2: Normal Q-Q
A Q-Q plot orders the residuals from smallest to largest and compares them to the quantiles they would have if they were perfectly normally distributed. The plot is essentially a scatter where each point is one residual: the horizontal coordinate is what the residual would be under perfect normality, and the vertical coordinate is what the residual actually is.
Points that fall along the diagonal mean the empirical and theoretical quantiles match, that is, the residuals are approximately normal. Points that curve away from the diagonal indicate deviation from normality, usually at the tails (heavy tails, light tails, or asymmetry).









The points sit close to the diagonal across the middle and most of the tails, with small deviations at the very extremes (typical and usually fine). Approximately normal.


20.2.3 Plot 3: Scale-Location
This is the residuals-vs-fitted plot transformed slightly: instead of raw residuals, the vertical axis shows the square root of the absolute standardized residuals. The transformation makes any change in the spread of the residuals easier to spot.
A horizontal smooth line with constant spread above and below it indicates homoscedasticity. An upward-sloping smooth line indicates heteroscedasticity (spread increases with fitted value); a downward slope means the opposite.









A near-flat red line is what we want. A clear upward or downward slope would indicate heteroscedasticity.


20.2.4 Plot 4: Residuals vs Leverage
The first three plots look at the residuals to diagnose general patterns. The fourth plot is different: it identifies particular observations that have an unusually large effect on the fit of the model, called influential observations.
Two ingredients are at work. Leverage measures how unusual an observation is in its predictor values: an observation far from the mean of the predictors has high leverage, because changing it would have a large impact on the slope. Residual measures whether the model fits that observation well. An observation with high leverage and a large residual is the dangerous combination; it can dominate the OLS estimate and pull the line away from where it would otherwise sit.
R draws Cook’s distance contours on this plot (the dashed lines). Points outside the 0.5 or 1 contour are usually worth examining.









In our data, no single observation has both high leverage and a very large residual. There is no point that dominates the fit. In a different dataset, an obvious outlier in the upper-right or lower-right corner of this plot would warrant a closer look.

title: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model
section: 20.3 What to do when an assumption is violated
text:
20.3 What to do when an assumption is violated
A short, practical decision tree:

Linearity violation. Try a polynomial term (e.g., I(x^2)), a log transformation of the predictor or outcome, or a generalized additive model (GAM) using the mgcv package.
Homoscedasticity violation. Use robust (heteroscedasticity-consistent) standard errors via the sandwich package, transform the outcome (often log), or use generalized least squares.
Normality violation, small sample. Consider bootstrapping the standard errors, or transforming the outcome.
Normality violation, large sample. Often tolerable for estimation. Be cautious with inference for extreme tails.
Independence violation. Switch to a model that respects the clustering, typically a multilevel model (the lme4 package; lmer() is the most common function).
Influential observations. Examine the cases individually. If they reflect data-entry errors, correct them. If they reflect real but unusual participants, report results with and without the cases.

The general advice: assumption violations are reasons to think more carefully, not reasons to panic. A mild violation is a reason to acknowledge a limitation in your report. A serious violation is a reason to use a different model.

title: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model
section: 20.4 Multicollinearity: when predictors carry the same information
text:
20.4 Multicollinearity: when predictors carry the same information
Multicollinearity is not one of the LINE assumptions, but it is a closely related diagnostic concern. It belongs in this chapter because it shows up only once you have several predictors in a model, and because it tends to surprise people the first time they meet it.
The problem. In Chapter 17 we noted that when two predictors in a multiple regression are correlated, each slope is interpreted as the unique contribution of that predictor, after the other predictors have been accounted for. The example was that hours_weekly and trait_hostility are mildly correlated, and their joint R-squared (about 0.20) was a little less than the sum of their separate R-squareds (7.2 + 11.6 = 18.8 percent). The two predictors carry partly overlapping information; the model apportions the overlap so that no piece is double-counted.
That was a mild case. What happens when two predictors are not mildly correlated, but strongly correlated, carrying nearly the same information? The problem is called multicollinearity. The word combines “multi” (more than one) with “collinearity” (lying on the same line). It refers to any situation where two or more predictors in a regression are so closely related to each other that the model has trouble separating their individual contributions.

20.4.1 The intuition
A short analogy. Imagine two coworkers who do the same job. If only one of them is in the office, you can clearly see what they contribute: their unique output is everything they produce. If both are in the office and do nearly the same work, you can still see the total output of the team, but you cannot tell which one to credit for any specific piece. The team-level performance is unambiguous; the individual contributions are not.
Multicollinearity is the same situation in a regression. When two predictors carry nearly the same information, the joint contribution to the outcome is well estimated, but the individual contributions of each predictor are not. The model has to apportion the shared variance between them, and because the shared variance is most of what either predictor has to offer, the apportionment is very sensitive to small fluctuations in the data. Each slope is estimated from the tiny “unique” piece of variance that one predictor has but the other does not, and that tiny piece is what determines the standard error of the slope. The smaller the unique piece, the larger the standard error.
The consequence: the joint model fits well (R-squared remains high), but each individual slope has a large standard error, sometimes flips sign relative to what you would expect, and is not stable across replications of the study.


20.4.2 A demonstration on vgames_study
Let us construct the situation deliberately. We will create a new variable trait_hostility_v2 that equals trait_hostility plus a small amount of random noise: a near-clone of the original.

set.seed(2025)
data$trait_hostility_v2 <- data$trait_hostility +
                           rnorm(nrow(data), mean = 0, sd = 0.10)

cor(data$trait_hostility, data$trait_hostility_v2)

[1] 0.9959603


The two predictors correlate at about 0.99: nearly perfect.
Now fit two models. The first uses only the original trait hostility:

m_simple <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility, data = data)
round(summary(m_simple)$coefficients, 3)

                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)        3.198      0.451   7.098        0
trait_hostility    0.492      0.125   3.942        0


The slope of trait_hostility is about 0.61 with a standard error of about 0.15. Clean and precise.
The second model adds the near-clone:

m_collinear <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility + trait_hostility_v2, data = data)
round(summary(m_collinear)$coefficients, 3)

                   Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)           3.185      0.452   7.048    0.000
trait_hostility       1.493      1.394   1.071    0.286
trait_hostility_v2   -0.998      1.384  -0.721    0.472


Look at what happened. Both trait_hostility and trait_hostility_v2 now have point estimates that are very different from the simple model, their standard errors are roughly an order of magnitude larger, and the two slopes may even have opposite signs. None of this reflects a substantive change in what the data are telling us: the joint R-squared is essentially identical to the simple model, because no new information is in the second predictor. But the individual slopes are now unstable and uninterpretable.
This is multicollinearity in action.


20.4.3 The diagnostic: the variance inflation factor (VIF)
The standard diagnostic for multicollinearity is the variance inflation factor (VIF). Each predictor in a multiple regression has its own VIF, a single number that measures how much that predictor’s standard error is inflated by its overlap with the other predictors. A VIF of 1 means no inflation (the predictor is uncorrelated with the others). A VIF of 4 means the standard error is twice as large as it would have been with no overlap. A VIF of 100 means the standard error is 10 times larger.
The function vif() from the car package computes the VIF for each predictor in a fitted lm() model.

library(car)
vif(m_collinear)

   trait_hostility trait_hostility_v2 
          124.0211           124.0211 


Both VIFs are extremely large in this artificial example, which is exactly what the diagnosis of severe multicollinearity looks like. Compare to the original two-predictor model from Chapter 17:

m_original <- lm(aggression ~ hours_weekly + trait_hostility, data = data)
vif(m_original)

   hours_weekly trait_hostility 
       1.002841        1.002841 


Both VIFs are close to 1, confirming that hours_weekly and trait_hostility carry mostly distinct information.
A rule of thumb commonly cited in psychology (Cohen et al., 2003; James et al., 2013):

VIF below 5: usually fine.
VIF between 5 and 10: a warning sign, worth investigating.
VIF above 10: serious multicollinearity; the individual slopes should not be interpreted.

These thresholds are conventions, not hard rules. A VIF of 4.5 in a small dataset is more worrying than a VIF of 6 in a large one, and the substantive judgment about whether the individual slopes are interpretable should weigh both the VIF and the sample size.


20.4.4 What to do about it
Three practical responses, in order of decreasing aggressiveness.
1. Drop one of the redundant predictors. If two predictors carry nearly the same information, you do not need both. Drop the one that is harder to interpret, less reliable, or less central to your research question. The simple model with the remaining predictor will give you a clean, interpretable slope.
2. Combine the redundant predictors into a single composite. If both predictors are intended to measure the same construct (for example, two scales of trait hostility, or two items on the same subscale), the standard move is to average them, or to standardize them and then average, into a single composite. Chapter 11 covered the mechanics of composite scores. The composite then enters the regression as a single predictor, and the multicollinearity problem disappears.
3. Keep both predictors and report the inflated standard errors honestly. Occasionally you may have a reason to keep two collinear predictors in the model: perhaps you are not interested in the individual slopes but only in the joint R-squared, or perhaps the substantive question requires both. In that case, the individual slopes should be interpreted with caution or not at all, the inflated standard errors should be reported clearly, and the joint contribution of the collinear set should be the focus of interpretation.
A more advanced option exists for severe cases: principal components regression and ridge regression both handle collinear predictors by transforming the predictor set or by penalizing the slopes. They are beyond the scope of this book; for typical psychology research situations, the three options above are usually sufficient.


20.4.5 A visual picture of multicollinearity
The clearest picture of why multicollinearity inflates standard errors is a shared-variance diagram. The figure compares the simple regression on the left with the multicollinear regression on the right.








Figure 20.1: Shared-variance diagrams comparing a simple regression (left) with a multicollinear regression (right). Each circle represents the variance of a variable; the overlap between two circles represents the variance they share. Left panel: simple regression of aggression on trait_hostility. The overlap area is the simple-regression R-squared. The slope of trait_hostility is estimated from its overlap with aggression relative to its own total area. Right panel: multicollinear regression in which trait_hostility and trait_hostility_v2 are nearly identical, shown as two heavily overlapping circles. The ‘unique to trait_hostility’ and ‘unique to trait_hostility_v2’ regions (the thin top and bottom crescents) are tiny, and each predictor’s individual slope must be estimated from these tiny areas alone. The joint contribution of the two predictors to aggression is well estimated (the combined overlap with aggression is similar to the left panel), but the individual slopes are not.





What the figure shows. On the left, trait_hostility and aggression overlap in a moderate region. The blue circle has a clean area outside the overlap (its “unique” area), and the slope of trait_hostility is estimated from the relationship between its unique area and the overlap with aggression.
On the right, trait_hostility and trait_hostility_v2 overlap each other almost entirely. The “unique to trait_hostility” area is the thin top crescent, and the “unique to trait_hostility_v2” area is the thin bottom crescent. Each individual slope is estimated from one of these thin slivers alone, which is why the standard errors are inflated and the slopes become unstable. At the same time, the joint overlap of the merged predictor region with aggression is similar in size to the left panel’s overlap, which is why the joint R-squared barely changed.
This is the geometric reason for the apparent paradox in the demonstration above: a model that fits the data well at the level of the whole set of predictors but fails to give interpretable estimates for any individual predictor.
crumbs: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model

title: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model
section: 20.5 Comparing models: R-squared, adjusted R-squared, and beyond
text:
20.5 Comparing models: R-squared, adjusted R-squared, and beyond
Once you have several candidate models, how do you compare them?
The simplest comparison is by R-squared: the proportion of variance explained by each. As Chapter 19 noted, R-squared (almost) always goes up when you add predictors, even useless ones, which makes it a poor tool for comparing models with different numbers of predictors.
Adjusted R-squared penalizes each additional predictor. The formula is
\[
R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1 - R^2) \cdot \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1},
\]
where \(n\) is the number of observations and \(p\) is the number of predictors. With more predictors, the denominator shrinks, the correction grows, and adjusted R-squared falls relative to R-squared. Only a predictor that improves the fit more than expected by chance will increase adjusted R-squared.
Looking at the models we have built on vgames_study.csv, side by side:

m1 <- lm(aggression ~ hours_weekly, data = data)
m2 <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility, data = data)
m3 <- lm(aggression ~ hours_weekly + trait_hostility, data = data)
m4 <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility * condition, data = data)

summary_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("hours_weekly",
            "trait_hostility",
            "hours_weekly + trait_hostility",
            "trait_hostility * condition (interaction)"),
  Predictors = c(1, 1, 2, 3),   # main + interaction count
  R_squared          = c(summary(m1)$r.squared,
                         summary(m2)$r.squared,
                         summary(m3)$r.squared,
                         summary(m4)$r.squared),
  Adj_R_squared      = c(summary(m1)$adj.r.squared,
                         summary(m2)$adj.r.squared,
                         summary(m3)$adj.r.squared,
                         summary(m4)$adj.r.squared)
)
summary_table

                                      Model Predictors  R_squared Adj_R_squared
1                              hours_weekly          1 0.07158788    0.06371998
2                           trait_hostility          1 0.11636615    0.10887772
3            hours_weekly + trait_hostility          2 0.19823192    0.18452648
4 trait_hostility * condition (interaction)          3 0.39264041    0.37693283


The interaction model has the highest R-squared (about 0.39) and the highest adjusted R-squared. Adding condition and an interaction term improved the fit more than the penalty for the extra predictors took away. By this criterion, the interaction model is preferred.
Two more measures worth knowing about but not detailing here.
AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion) are alternative model-comparison numbers. Both balance fit against complexity, with stronger penalties than adjusted R-squared. Smaller is better for both. The functions AIC(model) and BIC(model) return them. They are particularly useful when comparing non-nested models or models with many predictors.
Cross-validation is the gold standard for prediction-oriented model comparison: fit each model on part of the data, evaluate it on the held-out part, and pick the model that generalizes best. The caret and tidymodels packages provide implementations.

title: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model
section: 20.6 When the linear model is not enough
text:
20.6 When the linear model is not enough
Linear regression is powerful and applies to a wide range of psychology research questions. It is not universal. Here is a map of common problems that go beyond the standard linear model, with the type of model that addresses each.
Problem 1: Nonlinear relationships. The true relationship between predictor and outcome is curved, not straight. Tools: polynomial regression (add I(x^2) to the formula), log or square-root transformations, generalized additive models (GAMs) via the mgcv package, splines.
Problem 2: Nested or grouped data. Participants are clustered: students in classrooms, employees in companies, measurements within people over time. Tools: multilevel models / mixed-effects models / hierarchical linear models. The lme4 package (lmer()) is the standard.
Problem 3: Latent variables. You want to model constructs that are not directly observed (intelligence, motivation, anxiety) using several observed indicators. Tools: structural equation modeling (SEM), confirmatory factor analysis, exploratory factor analysis. The lavaan package in R.
Problem 4: Categorical outcomes. The outcome is a category (yes/no, survived/died, chose option A/B/C), not a number on a continuous scale. Tools: logistic regression for two categories, multinomial logistic regression for more. In R: glm(... , family = binomial) for logistic regression.
Problem 5: Small samples or unusual distributions. Very few observations, or seriously non-normal residuals, or unusual sampling structures. Tools: bootstrap methods, permutation tests, Bayesian estimation (the brms and rstanarm packages).
Problem 6: Outliers, leverage, robust estimation. A few extreme observations dominate the fit. Tools: robust regression (the MASS::rlm() function and the robustbase package), explicit outlier-handling strategies (Chapter 12).
For each of these, the modeling structure changes, but the underlying pillars are the same: you describe data with a model, you fit the model, you check the fit, and (in inference) you test hypotheses. The vocabulary you have built in Section 3 transfers, even when the specific machinery is new.

Knowing these tools exist is the goal. You do not need to learn them now; when you encounter a research problem that one of them solves, you have a starting point.

title: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model
text:
20.7 Closing Section 3
We started Section 3 with the idea that a model is a useful simplification of data, that the mean is the simplest possible model, and that everything else (regression, multiple regression, interactions) builds on the same logic of predictions and residuals. We end with a small set of practical habits:

Fit the model with lm() and read the coefficients you care about (Chapters 16-18).
Check the assumptions with plot(model) (this chapter), and either accept the mild violations or pick a different model for the serious ones (Chapter 19).
Compare models with adjusted R-squared, not raw R-squared, when they have different numbers of predictors (this chapter).
Remember that everything in Section 3 is description, not inference. The slopes and R-squared values describe the dataset you have. The question of whether the patterns generalize to a population, and the standard errors and p-values that try to answer that question, are a topic for a later section of the book.

These habits are the entry to applied statistical modeling in psychology. The chapters that follow Section 3 take the same models and ask the inferential questions; later sections still take the same models and ask the causal questions. The modeling framework you have learned here is the engine that drives the rest.
crumbs: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model

title: 20  Diagnostics, model fit, and the limits of your model
text:
20.8 Check your understanding
1. What does plot(model) produce when model is a fitted lm object?

 It fits four separate regression models. It generates four diagnostic plots: Residuals vs Fitted, Normal Q-Q, Scale-Location, and Residuals vs Leverage. Together these are used to check the linear-model assumptions and identify influential observations. It plots the predictor and the outcome. It runs cross-validation on the model.

2. The “Residuals vs Fitted” plot is mainly used to check which assumptions?

 Normality only. Independence only. Linearity and homoscedasticity (the spread of the residuals across fitted values). Influential observations only.

3. What does the Normal Q-Q plot check?

 Whether the raw outcome is normal. Whether the residuals are approximately normally distributed: points falling roughly on the diagonal indicate approximate normality; curving away (especially at the tails) indicates non-normality. Whether the slope is significantly different from zero. Whether the predictors are correlated with each other.

4. What is an “influential observation”?

 An observation that has a small leverage but a very large residual. An observation with both unusual predictor values (high leverage) and a large residual. Such observations can disproportionately affect the fitted line. The Residuals vs Leverage plot, especially with Cook's distance contours, helps identify them. Any observation whose residual is positive. Any observation collected on a Tuesday.

5. Why is adjusted R-squared usually preferred over raw R-squared for comparing models?

 It is identical to R-squared. It penalizes the model for each additional predictor. Unlike raw R-squared, it does not necessarily increase when you add a predictor; it only increases if the predictor improves the fit more than would be expected by chance. It is the natural tool for comparing models with different numbers of predictors. It is always larger than R-squared. It is the square of the adjusted slope.

6. You have 200 students nested within 10 classrooms. Independence is violated. What is the standard fix?

 Use a different programming language. Use a multilevel (mixed-effects) model that accounts for the clustering, typically via the lmer() function in the lme4 package. Standard OLS standard errors will be misleadingly small if independence is violated. Use a logistic regression instead. Ignore it; OLS is robust to all violations.

7. You want to model “intelligence” as a latent variable, measured by several test scores. Which family of models is most appropriate?

 Logistic regression. Multilevel models. Structural equation modeling (SEM), with software like lavaan in R. SEM is the standard tool for modeling latent variables (constructs measured indirectly through several indicators). Robust regression.

8. What is the most important caveat to remember as Section 3 closes?

 The chapter has shown how to make causal claims from regression coefficients. Everything in Section 3 is description: fitting models and quantifying fit on the dataset you have. Whether the patterns generalize to a population, and the standard errors and p-values that try to answer that question, belong to statistical inference and will be covered in a later section. The linear model can be applied to any research question without modification. Adjusted R-squared replaces all other model-comparison measures.

9. Two predictors in a multiple regression are correlated with each other at r = 0.97. What is the most likely consequence for the fitted model?

 The joint R-squared will drop to nearly zero because the model cannot fit the data when predictors are correlated. The joint R-squared will be similar to a single-predictor model, but each individual slope will have a large standard error and the slopes will be unstable across samples. This is multicollinearity and can be diagnosed with the variance inflation factor (VIF) from the car package. Both individual slopes will become statistically significant at p < .001 because the high correlation amplifies the apparent effect of each predictor on the outcome. The lm() function will refuse to fit the model and will return an error message about singular design matrices.

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
text:
21.1 Welcome to Section 4
Section 1 taught you how R works as a tool. Section 2 taught you how to clean and summarize a dataset. Section 3 taught you how to fit and interpret linear models, from the simplest one-number model (the mean) all the way to multiple regression with interactions and assumption diagnostics.
Throughout Section 3 we said the same thing many times, in slightly different words:
That gap is what Section 4 is about. It is the gap between what we observe in our data and what we want to say about a broader population that our data was drawn from. Closing that gap, or at least quantifying it honestly, is what statistical inference does. The four chapters that follow build up the machinery, the logic, the philosophy, and the practical disciplines that make inference possible.
This chapter is the first step. Before any p-values, any tests, any “is this effect real?” decisions, there is a more basic question: why is generalizing from one sample to a population such a hard problem in the first place, and what new ideas do we need to handle it? By the end of the chapter you will have:
The chapter is conceptual and visual. There is some R code, but it is used to simulate sampling distributions so you can see them with your own eyes. The math is light.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
text:
Everything in this section is description. We are describing the dataset we have. We are not (yet) making any claim about whether the effects we see hold in the wider world, in people we did not sample, in studies we have not run.




a clear understanding of why having “just one sample” is the central obstacle of inference,
the concept of sampling variability: why the same study, run twice, gives different answers,
the concept of the sampling distribution: the distribution of all the answers you would have gotten if you had run the study many times,
the standard error, the single most important number in inference,
the Central Limit Theorem, which is what makes inference practical, and
a connection back to the Std. Error column you saw in lm() output in Chapter 16 and pointedly ignored at the time.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
section: 21.2 The fundamental gap: what we care about vs. what we have
text:
21.2 The fundamental gap: what we care about vs. what we have
Every study you read or run is a sample. A sample of 120 university students in Innsbruck. A sample of 200 children in a school in Pisa. A sample of 47 patients in a clinic in Berlin. A sample of one researcher’s data. None of these samples is the thing that science actually cares about.
What science cares about is something larger and harder to define. It cares about all young adults (not just our 120), about all children of school age in Western Europe (not just our 200), about all patients with this disorder (not just our 47). The set of all the units about which we want to make a claim is called the population. The bit of the population we actually measured is called the sample.
This vocabulary is more than a label. It carries a conceptual point worth restating in different ways, because students consistently underestimate how strange the situation is.

The population parameter is a number that describes the population. The mean aggression of all the young adults the study could speak to. The slope of hours_weekly on aggression for all gamers, not just our 120. Population parameters exist (in principle) but we cannot observe them directly.
The sample statistic is the corresponding number computed from the sample. The mean aggression of our 120 participants. The slope from lm(aggression ~ hours_weekly, data = data) fitted to our 120. Sample statistics are observable; we computed them throughout Section 3.

The sample statistic is our estimate of the population parameter. It is not, in any normal sense, the population parameter itself. It is the closest we can get to the population parameter given the data we collected.
Take a concrete case. In our running example, the mean aggression of the 120 participants in vgames_study.csv is:

mean(data$aggression)

[1] 4.888333


So 4.89 (rounded). What does this number actually tell us?
It is the mean aggression of the 120 participants in our sample. It is not the mean aggression of “all young adults,” “all gamers,” “all participants in similar studies,” or any other population we might care about. The number 4.89 is what we measured in our sample. The number we want, the population mean, is something we have never seen and almost certainly differs from 4.89 to some unknown extent.
The same applies to every other statistic in Section 3. The slope of 0.08 for hours_weekly predicting aggression. The R-squared of 0.072 for that simple regression. The interaction slope of 0.60 in Chapter 18 between condition and trait hostility. Every one of those numbers was a sample statistic. None of them was the population parameter. They were our estimates of population parameters we cannot see.

An analogy. Imagine you want to know the average height of all adults in your country. You cannot line up everyone and measure them. So you pick 100 people, measure them, average their heights, and get 172 cm. The 172 is the sample mean. The thing you actually want to know, the average height of every adult in your country, is the population mean. You will never know that number exactly. Your 100-person sample average is your estimate of it.

This sounds obvious when you put it this way. But the consequence is not obvious. If you cannot directly observe the population parameter, how can you ever say anything useful about it? Why is statistics not just throwing up its hands and saying “we cannot know”?
The answer to that question is the entire content of this chapter, and indeed of inferential statistics as a whole. The answer is that even though we cannot see the population, we can reason carefully about how much our sample estimate would have varied if we had drawn a different sample. That reasoning is what gives us tools to make principled statements about the population, despite never observing it directly.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
section: 21.3 The sample is just one of many possible samples
text:
21.3 The sample is just one of many possible samples
Here is the question that opens the door.
Suppose you ran your video-game study and computed the sample mean aggression: 4.89. Now imagine you went out and ran the study again, recruiting a completely different set of 120 participants from the same population, running the same protocol, computing the same statistic. What number would you get?
The answer that beginners often expect is: “Well, 4.89, or near it.” This is wrong. The right answer is: “Some other number, almost certainly. Maybe 4.81. Maybe 5.02. Maybe 4.71. The new sample is made of different people, and different people have different aggression scores, so the new mean will be different.”
This difference is not a flaw in your measurement, not a mistake by the experimenter, not a sign that your study was poorly designed. It is an unavoidable consequence of working with samples. Every sample contains different individuals, and the statistic you compute on those individuals depends on who happened to be in the sample. We call this phenomenon sampling variability.
It is essential to understand that sampling variability is structural, not error in the everyday sense. The 4.89 you got was a real, correct answer for the 120 people you happened to measure. So is the 4.81 you might have gotten from a different 120. There is no “correct” sample mean; each sample has its own mean. The variability between them is something we have to think about and live with, not something we should try to make go away.

An analogy. Imagine a giant bowl filled with millions of balls. Some are heavy, some are light, but the average weight (across all the balls in the bowl) is some fixed number, say 100 grams. Now you reach in, blindfolded, and scoop out a handful of, say, 30 balls. The average weight of those 30 balls will be some number, close to 100 but probably not exactly 100. If you put them back and scoop a different 30, the new average will be some other number, also close to 100 but probably not exactly 100, and probably not exactly the same as the first scoop. You scoop a third time: a third average, slightly different from the first two. This is sampling variability. The bowl never changed. Your scoops did.

A short illustration in R will make this concrete. To do it without needing a real bowl of balls, we will pretend that the 120 participants in our vgames_study data are the entire population (in real life they are not, but the simulation will illustrate the idea). Then we will repeatedly draw smaller samples from this “population” and look at how the sample mean varies.

# Pretend the 120 observations in `data` are our population.
# Repeatedly draw a sample of 30, compute its mean, look at how the means vary.
set.seed(2025)
sample1 <- sample(data$aggression, size = 30)
sample2 <- sample(data$aggression, size = 30)
sample3 <- sample(data$aggression, size = 30)

mean(sample1)

[1] 5.1

mean(sample2)

[1] 5.11

mean(sample3)

[1] 4.28


Each line draws a fresh sample of 30 from the same 120 observations, and computes the mean. The three means are not the same. They are close to each other and close to the overall mean of the data, but each one is its own number. That difference between the three numbers is sampling variability, made visible in a single line of R.









The five sample means in the plot above are all close to the population mean (the dashed line), but no two are identical. None of them equals the population mean exactly. Each sample sits in its own slightly different place. The dance around the truth, sample by sample, is the central object of inferential statistics.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
section: 21.4 Imagining many possible samples: the sampling distribution
text:
21.4 Imagining many possible samples: the sampling distribution
The next step is conceptually the most important in this chapter. The previous section showed that a sample mean is one number among many possible numbers, because different samples produce different means. The natural next question is: what does the collection of all those possible numbers look like? If we could somehow take every possible sample of 120 people from the population, compute the mean of each, and stack them all up, what would the result look like?
The collection of all the values a statistic could take, across all the possible samples one could draw from the population, is called the sampling distribution of that statistic.
This is a slippery concept on first encounter, because the sampling distribution is something we are imagining. We do not actually draw all those samples; we draw one sample, in practice. But the idea of the sampling distribution is the bridge between our single sample and the population we care about. It tells us how much our particular sample mean could have varied from other possible means we did not happen to draw.
Three properties of the sampling distribution matter most:

The center. Across all possible samples, the average value of the sample mean equals the population mean. The sampling distribution is centered exactly on the population parameter. This is true even though most individual samples will not give exactly the population value. Some samples land too low, some land too high; on average they balance.
The spread. The sampling distribution has a width. Some sample means land far from the population value, some land close. The spread tells us how much “wobble” there is from sample to sample.
The shape. For most reasonable statistics, the sampling distribution looks like a bell curve, even when the underlying data does not. We will come to why this is true in a later section; the fact alone matters now.

It is helpful to compare the sampling distribution to two other distributions that are easy to confuse with it.

The population distribution is the distribution of values among all units in the population. The histogram of aggression scores for all the young adults we are interested in. It exists in principle. We almost never see it directly.
The sample distribution is the distribution of values in our specific sample. The histogram of aggression scores for our 120 participants. We can see this; we can plot it; we have done it many times already.
The sampling distribution is the distribution of the statistic (the mean, say, or a slope) across all possible samples. It is not a distribution of raw values; it is a distribution of summaries. It exists only in our imagination unless we manually simulate it.

The three are easy to mix up because they all involve histograms and they all involve the same population. But they are distinct objects.








Distribution
Each point is
Where we see it




Population distribution
One unit (e.g., one person)
Almost never observed


Sample distribution
One unit in our sample
Directly: hist(data$aggression)


Sampling distribution
One summary statistic (e.g., the mean) from one hypothetical sample
Imagined; can be simulated



The sampling distribution is the new object in this section, and the rest of the chapter builds up tools to think about it. The next step is to actually look at one, by simulating it.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
section: 21.5 Building a sampling distribution by simulation
text:
21.5 Building a sampling distribution by simulation
We cannot in practice run a real study a thousand times. But we can do something almost as good in R: we can build a fake population on the computer, draw a thousand samples from it, compute the mean of each, and plot the resulting collection of means. That collection is the sampling distribution. By looking at it directly, we can see all three properties listed above with our own eyes.
The R function for generating random numbers from a normal distribution is rnorm(). If we wanted to pretend that aggression in some population was normally distributed with a mean of 5.0 and a standard deviation of 1.5, we could generate one sample of 30 like this:

set.seed(2025)
one_sample <- rnorm(30, mean = 5.0, sd = 1.5)
mean(one_sample)

[1] 5.310186


So one sample of 30 from the population gave us a sample mean of about 5.06. As we already know, a different sample would give us a different mean. The function replicate() lets us repeat that operation many times automatically. The following line draws 1000 different samples of size 30 from the same population, computing the mean of each:

set.seed(2025)
sample_means <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(30, mean = 5.0, sd = 1.5)))
length(sample_means)

[1] 1000

head(sample_means)

[1] 5.310186 5.094302 4.763600 4.664535 4.495557 5.259209


We now have a vector of 1000 sample means. Each one is the mean of a different sample of 30 people from the same population. The first six values are shown.
What does the distribution of these 1000 means look like? Two things, mainly: where is its center, and how spread out is it?

mean(sample_means)

[1] 4.995496

sd(sample_means)

[1] 0.2841269


The mean of our 1000 sample means is very close to 5.0, the value we set when we generated the population. The standard deviation of those 1000 sample means is around 0.27. These are the central tendency and the spread of the sampling distribution. Let us visualize it:









Look closely at this plot. Every bar represents how many of our 1000 simulated samples produced a mean in that small bin. The dashed red line is the true population mean. Notice:

The histogram is centered on the population mean (5.0). Some sample means landed a little below; some landed a little above. The average of all 1000 sample means is essentially 5.0. This is the “center” property of the sampling distribution.
The histogram is bell-shaped. It rises smoothly from the tails to a peak near 5.0 and falls smoothly back down. This is the “shape” property. The Central Limit Theorem (next major section) tells us this shape is approximately always the case.
The histogram has a width. Sample means ranged roughly from 4.3 to 5.7. The vast majority sit between about 4.5 and 5.5. The standard deviation of the 1000 sample means (about 0.27) measures this width.

A single sample is one draw from this distribution. The mean of our actual study is one of the dots that would fall somewhere on this histogram. The 1000 dots in our simulation are alternative versions of that one dot, each from a different hypothetical replication.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
text:
21.6 The standard error: quantifying precision
The width of the sampling distribution has a special name: the standard error (SE) of the statistic. It is just the standard deviation of the sampling distribution. Its meaning is the meaning of that width.

A small standard error means the sampling distribution is narrow. The statistic does not vary much across samples. Our estimate is precise: we would expect to get a similar answer if we ran the study again.
A large standard error means the sampling distribution is wide. The statistic varies a lot across samples. Our estimate is imprecise: a new sample could easily give a substantially different answer.

The standard error is not a property of the data we collected. It is a property of the procedure (the statistic + the sample size + the population variability). The same data could yield estimates with different standard errors depending on which statistic you compute (the mean has one SE, the median has another, a slope has another). And the same statistic on the same kind of data could yield different SEs depending on the sample size.
For the sample mean specifically, there is a tidy formula:
\[
SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
In words: the standard error of the sample mean equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. The formula captures two intuitions cleanly:

The standard error grows with σ. If the data are very variable (people differ a lot from each other), then a fixed-size sample will reflect that variability in its estimate of the mean. SE goes up.
The standard error shrinks with n. Larger samples produce more precise estimates. Doubling the sample size does not, however, halve the SE; because of the square root, you need to quadruple the sample size to halve the SE.

Our simulation matches the formula. The population SD was 1.5, the sample size was 30, so we expected the SE to be:

1.5 / sqrt(30)

[1] 0.2738613


And the standard deviation of our 1000 simulated means was about 0.27. The two values agree to within simulation noise. The formula is not magic; it is the analytic shortcut for the same quantity our simulation produced by brute force.

21.6.1 Watching the standard error shrink with sample size
We can visualize the “n shrinks the SE” point directly by running the simulation at several sample sizes and overlaying the resulting sampling distributions.

set.seed(2025)
means_n10  <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(10,  mean = 5.0, sd = 1.5)))
means_n30  <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(30,  mean = 5.0, sd = 1.5)))
means_n100 <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(100, mean = 5.0, sd = 1.5)))
means_n500 <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(500, mean = 5.0, sd = 1.5)))

# Empirical SE (standard deviation of the sample means)
c(n10 = sd(means_n10), n30 = sd(means_n30),
  n100 = sd(means_n100), n500 = sd(means_n500))

       n10        n30       n100       n500 
0.47221669 0.28212384 0.14866981 0.06651027 

# Theoretical SE from the formula
c(n10 = 1.5 / sqrt(10), n30 = 1.5 / sqrt(30),
  n100 = 1.5 / sqrt(100), n500 = 1.5 / sqrt(500))

       n10        n30       n100       n500 
0.47434165 0.27386128 0.15000000 0.06708204 


The simulated and theoretical SEs agree, and you can see the SE shrinking from about 0.47 (n = 10) down to about 0.067 (n = 500). The same comparison as a single picture:









All four sampling distributions are centered on 5.0 (the population mean, marked with a dashed line). But they get progressively narrower as the sample size increases. With n = 10, the sample means range from about 3.5 to 6.5; with n = 500, they range from roughly 4.85 to 5.15. The center is the same; the precision (the SE) is what changes.


21.6.2 The connection back to lm() output
Recall the summary(lm(...)) output from Chapter 16. The Coefficients block had four columns: Estimate, Std. Error, t value, and Pr(>|t|). We told you, every time, to focus on the Estimate column and to ignore the rest until Section 4.
You can now read the second column. The Std. Error of a coefficient is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of that coefficient. It tells you how much the slope (or intercept) would wobble if you re-ran the study with a fresh sample of the same size from the same population. A small Std. Error means the slope is a precise estimate; a large Std. Error means it is imprecise. The remaining two columns (the t-value and the p-value) are calculations built on top of this Std. Error; they answer the question “is the slope big enough, relative to its noise, that we should treat it as different from zero?” That is Chapter 22’s topic. The Std. Error, the building block, is what we have just defined.
For example, on our running model:

m1 <- lm(aggression ~ hours_weekly, data = data)
summary(m1)$coefficients

               Estimate Std. Error  t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  4.19617633  0.2698749 15.54860 2.432180e-30
hours_weekly 0.08164636  0.0270674  3.01641 3.133333e-03


The slope of hours_weekly is 0.082, and its Std. Error is 0.027. The interpretation: if we re-ran the same study many times with fresh samples of 120, the slope estimates would cluster around the true population slope, with a typical wobble (standard deviation) of about 0.027. The slope estimate is reasonably precise, in the sense that it would not bounce around all over the place across replications.

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
section: 21.7 The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): why the bell curve is so important
text:
21.7 The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): why the bell curve is so important
We have been quietly relying on a fact whose strength we have not yet stated: the sampling distribution was always bell-shaped, no matter what we tried. We generated the underlying data from a normal distribution in those examples, which makes the bell shape unsurprising. But the result is much stronger than that.
The Central Limit Theorem says: when you compute the mean of a sample, the sampling distribution of that mean is approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the original data, as long as the sample is large enough.
This is a theorem, in the strong mathematical sense. It has a proof. It is not an approximation or a rule of thumb. It says that even if the underlying data is wildly skewed, bimodal, or strangely shaped, the means of large enough samples behave as if they were drawn from a normal distribution. Means smooth out the strangeness of the original data.
The phrase “large enough” is the only fuzzy part. How large is enough depends on how non-normal the original data is. A common practical rule of thumb is n ≥ 30, but this is just a rule, not a law. With mildly non-normal data, samples of 20 or 25 give close-to-normal sampling distributions. With severely skewed or weird data, you may need 50 or more before the sampling distribution is convincingly normal.
A demonstration helps. Suppose the underlying data were not normal at all, but were drawn from a heavily skewed distribution (a chi-squared distribution, say, which has a long tail to the right). What does the sampling distribution of the mean look like as we increase n?


















The first picture above shows the population, which is heavily skewed to the right. Most values are low, but a long tail extends to the right. The second picture shows what the sampling distribution of the mean looks like for that population at four sample sizes.

With n = 2, the sampling distribution still looks skewed: averaging just two values is not enough to smooth out the population’s asymmetry.
With n = 5, the skew is much weaker but visible.
With n = 30, the sampling distribution looks essentially normal. The population’s skew has been smoothed out by averaging 30 values at a time.
With n = 200, the sampling distribution is normal, narrow, and tightly centered on the true population mean.

This is the CLT at work. The shape of the data (top panel) and the shape of the sampling distribution of the mean (bottom panel) are very different things. As n grows, the sampling distribution becomes more and more normal, regardless of how non-normal the data themselves are.
Why does this matter? Because the normal distribution has known mathematical properties that we can use to compute probabilities (and therefore p-values, in the next chapter). If sampling distributions were arbitrarily shaped, we could not compute anything; every problem would need bespoke math. The CLT guarantees that as long as our samples are reasonably large, we can use the normal distribution as the reference shape for our statistic. This is the single largest reason the normal distribution shows up everywhere in statistics.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
section: 21.8 This applies to everything, not just means
text:
21.8 This applies to everything, not just means
We have been computing the sampling distribution of the sample mean because the mean is the simplest statistic and the easiest to visualize. But the concept of a sampling distribution is not specific to means. It applies to every statistic you can compute from a sample.

The sampling distribution of a regression slope describes how the slope would vary across hypothetical replications.
The sampling distribution of an R-squared describes how R-squared would vary.
The sampling distribution of a correlation coefficient describes how the correlation would vary.
The sampling distribution of a difference between two group means describes how the difference would vary.
The sampling distribution of any statistic you can compute is the distribution of that statistic across all possible samples.

The standard error is, for every one of these, the standard deviation of the corresponding sampling distribution. The Std. Error column of summary(lm(...)) contains the standard errors of the coefficients. When R prints the standard error of a correlation, or of a chi-squared statistic, or of a regression slope, the meaning is the same: the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of that statistic.
You will eventually meet two refinements of this idea.

For some statistics, the sampling distribution is approximately normal (CLT applies). For others, it has a specific, known shape (the t, F, or chi-squared distributions). Which shape applies depends on the statistic and on what is known about the data. We will return to this when we look at test statistics in Chapter 23.
The shape of the sampling distribution is what lets us compute p-values. A p-value is the probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as ours, assuming a particular value of the population parameter. To compute that probability, we need to know what the sampling distribution looks like under that assumption. This is exactly what makes the work of Chapter 22 possible.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
section: 21.9 Why is all of this so important?
text:
21.9 Why is all of this so important?
We started the chapter with a complaint: we care about the population, but we have only a sample. The number we computed from our sample (the mean, the slope, the R-squared) is not the population parameter; it is one observation in a large space of possible numbers we could have computed if we had drawn a different sample.
The sampling distribution is the entire object that describes that space. The standard error is the single number that summarizes how wide the space is. Together, they let us say things like:

“Our estimated slope is 0.08, with an SE of 0.03. The sampling distribution of slopes from studies like this is bell-shaped and centered on the true population slope. So if the true slope were zero, results as far from zero as 0.08 would be unusual (because 0.08 is much bigger than 0.03).”
“Our estimated mean is 4.89, with an SE of 0.14. If we ran the study many times, our means would mostly land between roughly 4.61 and 5.17 (about 2 SE above and below). So the population mean is plausibly anywhere in that range; we cannot pin it down more precisely than that.”

These statements are inferences. They are the kind of claim that statistical inference is in the business of producing. To make them, you need the sampling distribution as a conceptual object, and you need the standard error as a quantitative summary. The rest of Section 4 will take this foundation and build on it: how do we decide whether a result is too far from zero to be plausibly chance? What does “too far” mean precisely? What are the rules of the game, and how were they invented? Those are the topics of Chapters 22 onwards.
For Lakens’ formulation of this same idea, see Chapter 1 of Improving Your Statistical Inferences (Lakens, 2022). Navarro (2018), Chapter 9 (Introduction to probability) and Chapter 10 (Estimating unknown quantities from a sample), covers the same material from a slightly different angle and is a useful companion read.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
text:
21.10 Looking ahead
Chapter 22 picks up where this one leaves off. We have a sample statistic, and we know its sampling distribution. The natural next question is: how should we use this to make a decision about whether an effect in our data is “real” in the population? That question has a long, contested history. Two giants of twentieth-century statistics, Ronald Fisher and Jerzy Neyman (with Egon Pearson), proposed two different answers, and psychology has been using a strange mixture of both ever since. Chapter 22 walks through that history, names the two frameworks, and tells you precisely what a p-value is (and, more importantly, what it is not). It is the chapter that connects the standard error you now understand to the p-values you will read in every research paper for the rest of your career.
crumbs: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error

title: 21  Why inference? Samples, populations, and the standard error
text:
21.11 Check your understanding
1. What is the difference between a population and a sample, and between a population parameter and a sample statistic?

 The population is the dataset the experimenter measured; the sample is a subset of it shown in graphs. The population is the full set of units we want to make claims about; the sample is the subset of units we actually measured. The population is the variables in the data; the sample is the participants who answered them. The population is the larger version of the sample; the two contain the same individuals.

2. What is “sampling variability”?

 Random measurement error introduced by the experimenter that better instruments would remove. A bias in the sample that should be corrected by adjusting the data before analysis. The structural variation of a sample statistic across different samples from the same population; even a perfect study gives a different answer each time. A computational artifact of statistical software that disappears with more accurate algorithms.

3. What is the sampling distribution of a statistic?

 The distribution of the raw data values across all units in the population. The distribution of the raw data values across the units in our specific sample. The distribution of a statistic (such as the sample mean) across all the possible samples one could draw from the population. The distribution of the predictor variables included in a regression model.

4. Where is the sampling distribution of the sample mean centered?

 On the value of the largest observation in the sample. On zero, regardless of the population parameter, by mathematical construction. On the population parameter, even though individual samples almost never land exactly there. On the value of the most recent sample, which shifts the distribution each time.

5. What is the standard error (SE) of a statistic?

 The standard deviation of the raw data values in our sample. The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the statistic; it quantifies the precision of our estimate. A correction factor applied to p-values when model assumptions are violated. The largest absolute value the statistic could plausibly take in any sample.

6. How does sample size affect the standard error?

 Larger samples produce larger SEs, because they contain more information about variation. Larger samples produce smaller SEs, because averaging over more observations smooths out individual variation; for the mean, SE = σ / √n. Sample size has no effect on the SE; only the variability of the population determines it. Smaller samples produce smaller SEs, because they avoid the chance of including extreme values.

7. What does the Central Limit Theorem say?

 The raw data of any analysis must be normally distributed before computing any statistic. For large enough samples, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the raw data. The sample size must be exactly 30 for the theorem to apply; smaller and larger values invalidate it. Only means computed from already-normal data have sampling distributions; other statistics do not.

8. Does the concept of a sampling distribution apply only to means?

 Only the sample mean has a sampling distribution; other statistics do not. Only statistics from normally distributed data have a sampling distribution. Every statistic computed from a sample has a sampling distribution: slopes, correlations, R-squared, group differences, and so on. Sampling distributions are only meaningful when the population contains millions of units.

9. What does the “Std. Error” column of an lm() model’s coefficients table represent?

 The variability of the predictor variable across observations in the dataset. The estimated standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the slope across hypothetical replications of the study. The residual standard error of the regression model around the fitted line. The correlation between the predictor and the outcome variable in the sample.

10. Why does the sampling distribution matter for statistical inference?

 Knowing the sampling distribution lets us read p-values directly off the data. It lets us reason about how plausible our sample value is under different hypotheses about the population, despite never observing the population directly. The sampling distribution is only useful when the exact population values are already known. The sampling distribution replaces the need for descriptive statistics in research reports.

title: 22  P-values, Fisher, and Neyman-Pearson
text:
22.1 Where we are
Chapter 21 established the basic objects of statistical inference. We have a sample. The statistic we compute from that sample (a mean, a slope, a correlation) is one number out of many we could have gotten with a different sample. The collection of all those possible numbers is the sampling distribution, and its standard deviation is the standard error. With the Central Limit Theorem, we know what the sampling distribution looks like for most reasonable statistics: roughly normal, centered on the true population value, with a width quantified by the SE.
We are now ready to ask the question every researcher actually wants to answer: given my one sample, can I conclude that the effect I see is real in the population, or could it be a fluke?
That question has a longer and more contested history than most textbooks admit. Twentieth-century statistics produced two different answers, by two different teams of statisticians, that look superficially similar but are deeply different in what they promise and what they ask of you. Psychology and most empirical sciences inherited a strange hybrid of both, and a lot of the confusion around p-values that you encounter in research papers is due to that hybrid. This chapter walks you through:
The chapter is heavy on concepts and light on R code. The arithmetic is one short equation; the philosophy is everything.

title: 22  P-values, Fisher, and Neyman-Pearson
text:
