title: 33  Visualizing distributions
text:
33.1 Histograms
This chapter is about visualizing the shape of a single continuous variable. Where Chapter 31 focused on showing means and spread, this chapter focuses on showing the whole distribution: where the values cluster, where they thin out, whether they are symmetric or skewed, whether there are multiple modes, whether outliers sit far from the central mass.
Distribution plots are useful for several reasons. They reveal features that summary statistics like the mean and SD hide. They help diagnose whether a particular analysis is appropriate (a t-test on a heavily skewed outcome is suspect, for instance). They communicate the underlying data to the reader in a way that bar plots and means cannot. And, as we will see in the final section, the visual comparison of two overlapping distributions is a direct intuition pump for standardized effect sizes like Cohen’s d.
We use the vgames_study data throughout.
The most basic distribution plot is the histogram. It divides the range of the variable into bins of equal width, counts the observations in each bin, and shows the counts as adjacent bars.
ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Aggression", y = "Number of participants") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 33.1
The choice of bin width matters. Too few bins (a wide binwidth) smooths over real features of the distribution. Too many bins (a narrow binwidth) shows random noise as if it were structure. The figure below shows the same data with three different bin widths.
p_wide <- ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "binwidth = 2 (too coarse)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

p_good <- ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "binwidth = 0.5 (reasonable)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

p_narrow <- ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "binwidth = 0.1 (too narrow)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

if (requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  patchwork::wrap_plots(p_wide, p_good, p_narrow, ncol = 3)
} else {
  gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_wide, p_good, p_narrow, ncol = 3)
}







Figure 33.2
A useful rule of thumb is to start with a binwidth that places about 20 to 30 bars across the range of the data, then adjust by eye. There is no objectively correct bin width; the right choice depends on what features of the distribution you want to communicate.
The y-axis of a histogram is “count” by default. Use aes(y = after_stat(density)) to switch to a density y-axis, which scales the histogram so that the total area sums to 1. This is the right choice when you want to overlay theoretical distributions or compare histograms across datasets with different sample sizes.
ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression, y = after_stat(density))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Aggression", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 33.3
The shape is identical to the count histogram; only the y-axis scaling has changed.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 33  Visualizing distributions
text:
33.2 Density plots
A density plot is a smoothed version of a histogram. Instead of binning into discrete bars, it estimates a continuous curve that represents the underlying density of the data. The function geom_density() produces it.

ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4,
               color = "steelblue4", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Aggression", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 33.4





Density plots are useful when the histogram’s binning starts to feel arbitrary. They show the general shape (peaks, tails, skew) without the visual noise of discrete bars. The trade-off is that the smoothing involves a choice (the bandwidth, controlled by bw or adjust), and a poor bandwidth choice can either oversmooth (hiding real features) or undersmooth (showing noise as if it were structure). Same trade-off as the histogram, just with a different name for the parameter.
The clearest situation in which density beats histogram is when you want to overlay multiple groups on the same plot. Histograms get visually crowded when stacked; densities can sit on top of each other with transparency without losing clarity.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 33  Visualizing distributions
text:
33.3 Overlapping density plots
To compare the distributions of a variable across two or more groups, plot the density for each group on the same axes, with semi-transparent fills so both are visible where they overlap.

ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression, fill = condition,
                   color = condition)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Aggression", y = "Density",
       fill = "Condition", color = "Condition") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 33.5





The visual story is immediately readable: the violent-condition density (one color) is shifted to the right compared to the neutral-condition density (the other color). The shaded overlap shows where the two distributions cover the same values; the non-overlapping tails show where each distribution has data the other does not.
Overlapping density plots are one of the most informative visualizations available for comparing two groups. They show the means (where each curve peaks), the spread (how wide each curve is), the shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal), and the overlap (how distinguishable the two groups are). Five summary statistics are visible at a glance in one figure.
The same approach works for more than two groups, with one important caveat: if there are too many groups, the layered densities become a mess. Three or four groups is usually the practical maximum for overlapping densities. For more, switch to ridgeline plots (next section).
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 33  Visualizing distributions
text:
33.4 Ridgeline plots
A ridgeline plot (also called a “joyplot”, in reference to the album cover for Joy Division’s Unknown Pleasures) shows multiple distributions stacked vertically, with each distribution offset from the next so they can all be seen simultaneously without obscuring each other. It is the right choice when there are many groups to compare.
Ridgeline plots are produced by the ggridges package. Let us first construct an illustrative grouping: bin participants by age into four categories.

vgames$age_bin <- cut(vgames$age,
                      breaks = c(17, 22, 26, 30, 36),
                      labels = c("18-22", "23-26",
                                 "27-30", "31-35"))

if (requireNamespace("ggridges", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(ggridges)
  ggplot(vgames, aes(x = aggression, y = age_bin,
                     fill = age_bin)) +
    geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.6, color = "white",
                        scale = 1.1, rel_min_height = 0.01) +
    labs(x = "Aggression", y = "Age band",
         fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
} else {
  cat("(ggridges not installed; on your machine the figure would show\n")
  cat("four overlapping density curves, one per age band, stacked vertically.)\n")
}







Figure 33.6





Each band of the figure is a density estimate of aggression for participants of that age. Stacking them vertically lets the eye scan from top to bottom and quickly compare how the distribution changes across categories. A clean ridgeline plot can replace five or six small-multiples panels in a single visualization.
The scale argument controls how much the densities overlap vertically; values larger than 1 produce more overlap, smaller values less. The rel_min_height argument hides density tails below a threshold to clean up the plot.
Ridgeline plots are a relatively recent addition to the standard data-visualization toolkit, popularized by Allen, Poggiali, Whitaker, Marshall, van Langen, and Kievit (2021) as part of a broader “raincloud” plot family that combines density, boxplot, and individual-point elements.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 33  Visualizing distributions
section: 33.5 Visualizing standardized effect sizes with overlapping densities
text:
33.5 Visualizing standardized effect sizes with overlapping densities
Overlapping density plots are not just descriptive tools; they are the most intuitive visualization available for the standardized effect sizes we have used throughout Section 4. Cohen’s d is essentially a measure of how far apart two distributions are, expressed in standard-deviation units. The visual fingerprint of d is exactly how separated two overlapping densities look.
The figure below shows the same two normal distributions, separated by Cohen’s d values of 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.5, and 2.0.

d_vals <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1.5, 2.0)

# Build six panels of two-distribution data
build_panel <- function(d) {
  x <- seq(-4, 4 + d, length.out = 400)
  rbind(
    data.frame(x = x, density = dnorm(x, mean = 0, sd = 1),
               group = "Group A"),
    data.frame(x = x, density = dnorm(x, mean = d, sd = 1),
               group = "Group B")
  ) |>
    mutate(facet = sprintf("d = %.1f", d))
}

grid_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(d_vals, build_panel))
grid_df$facet <- factor(grid_df$facet,
                        levels = sprintf("d = %.1f", d_vals))

ggplot(grid_df, aes(x = x, y = density, fill = group, color = group)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.35, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ facet, ncol = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Group A" = "steelblue",
                               "Group B" = "darkorange")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Group A" = "steelblue4",
                                "Group B" = "darkorange3")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       fill = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))







Figure 33.7





Reading the figure from left to right: at d = 0.2 the two distributions are almost identical; at d = 0.5 they are visibly distinct but heavily overlapping; at d = 0.8 the overlap is meaningful but the means are clearly separated; at d = 1.5 the overlap is much reduced; at d = 2.0 the distributions are essentially separated, with only a small overlap in the tails. Memorizing this grid is one of the most useful effect-size intuitions a researcher can develop. When a paper reports d = 0.6, you should be able to picture the corresponding amount of overlap without doing any calculation.
The arrow annotation below shows the same idea on a single panel: Cohen’s d is the distance between the means, measured in standard-deviation units.

x_d <- seq(-4, 5, length.out = 400)
df_d <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = x_d, density = dnorm(x_d, mean = 0, sd = 1),
             group = "Group A"),
  data.frame(x = x_d, density = dnorm(x_d, mean = 0.8, sd = 1),
             group = "Group B")
)

ggplot(df_d, aes(x = x, y = density,
                 fill = group, color = group)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.35, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, 0.8), linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, xend = 0.8,
           y = 0.45, yend = 0.45,
           arrow = grid::arrow(ends = "both",
                               length = unit(0.15, "cm")),
           color = "grey20") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.4, y = 0.49,
           label = "d = 0.8 SDs",
           size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Group A" = "steelblue",
                               "Group B" = "darkorange")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Group A" = "steelblue4",
                                "Group B" = "darkorange3")) +
  labs(x = "Outcome", y = "Density",
       fill = NULL, color = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.55)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank())







Figure 33.8





The dashed vertical lines mark the means of the two distributions. The horizontal arrow between them, in standard-deviation units, is Cohen’s d. The shaded overlap is the part of the two distributions that occupy the same range of outcome values. Pieces of intuition that fall directly out of this picture:

A small Cohen’s d means a small distance between the means relative to the SD. The means are close compared to the spread of either group.
A large Cohen’s d means the opposite. The means are well separated relative to the spread of either group.
The amount of overlap is not the same as the amount of variance explained, but is closely related to it. Roughly, overlap shrinks as d grows.
Even at d = 2.0, the distributions still overlap. Individual observations from the lower-mean group can exceed the mean of the higher-mean group, just less often. This is why standardized effect sizes do not predict individual-level differences with certainty (recall the discussion in Chapter 27, section 27.5).

When you see Cohen’s d in a paper from now on, look at the grid in figure 33.5 first, find the closest value, and that picture is what the data look like. The figure does much of the interpretive work for you.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 33  Visualizing distributions
text:
33.6 Check your understanding
1. How does the choice of bin width affect a histogram, and what is a reasonable default?

 The choice of binwidth in a histogram is purely cosmetic and has no effect on the visual interpretation of the underlying distribution, because the same data are being displayed regardless of how many bars are shown. The choice of binwidth in a histogram affects whether real features of the distribution are visible or hidden: too-wide bins smooth over genuine structure, while too-narrow bins display random noise as if it were structure, and the right choice depends on what the figure is meant to communicate. The choice of binwidth in a histogram is determined automatically by ggplot2 using a default algorithm that always produces the optimal representation of the data, so users should never specify the binwidth manually. The choice of binwidth in a histogram is constrained by the sample size and cannot be adjusted independently, because the formula for binwidth selection includes the number of observations as a fixed input.

2. What is the relationship between a density plot and a histogram?

 A density plot is always a more accurate representation of the underlying data than a histogram because the smoothing procedure removes random sampling noise and reveals the true population distribution from which the sample was drawn. A density plot replaces the discrete bars of a histogram with a continuous smoothed curve, which is useful for showing general shape without the visual noise of bars; the smoothing involves a bandwidth choice that has the same kind of trade-off (oversmoothing vs undersmoothing) as the binwidth choice in a histogram. A density plot and a histogram are mathematically equivalent representations of the same data, with the density plot using a continuous y-axis that always integrates to 1 and the histogram using a discrete y-axis of integer counts. A density plot can only be used for normally distributed data because the smoothing procedure used by geom_density() assumes a Gaussian kernel and produces misleading results for skewed or multimodal distributions.

3. What information does an overlapping density plot of two groups convey, and what is its practical limit on the number of groups?

 Overlapping density plots are appropriate only when the groups are perfectly normally distributed with equal variances, otherwise the overlap area is not interpretable as a measure of similarity between the groups. Overlapping density plots show the means, spreads, shapes, and overlap of two or more groups in a single figure, making them one of the most informative comparisons available, with three or four groups being the practical maximum before the layered curves become visually unreadable. Overlapping density plots can only display two groups at a time, because adding a third density would require a separate axis and would invalidate the visual comparison of the first two distributions. Overlapping density plots are equivalent to side-by-side box plots and convey exactly the same information; the choice between them is a matter of personal preference rather than the kind of insight the figure provides.

4. What does a ridgeline plot show and when is it preferable to an overlapping density plot?

 Ridgeline plots are an outdated form of distributional visualization that has been superseded by the more efficient overlapping density plot in modern ggplot2 workflows. Ridgeline plots stack multiple density estimates vertically with each distribution offset from the next, allowing many groups to be compared simultaneously without the visual crowding that overlapping density plots suffer when more than three or four groups are shown. Ridgeline plots show one density per category but require all categories to have the same sample size, otherwise the relative heights of the densities cannot be compared across rows. Ridgeline plots display the cumulative distribution function rather than the density, so the interpretation of any individual ridge corresponds to the proportion of observations below each value rather than the density at that value.

5. How does Cohen’s d relate to the visual overlap of two density distributions?

 Cohen's d is computed from the area of overlap between two distributions, so a Cohen's d of 0.5 corresponds to two distributions whose total overlapping area is 50%. Cohen's d is the distance between two means expressed in standard-deviation units, and the visual fingerprint of d is exactly how separated two overlapping distributions look; the grid of d values from 0.2 to 2.0 is a useful intuition pump for what each magnitude implies about overlap. Cohen's d measures the difference between two means in raw units of the outcome variable, so a Cohen's d of 0.5 always corresponds to a half-point difference on whatever scale the outcome is measured. Cohen's d is meaningful only for normally distributed outcomes with equal variances, and is undefined for the overlapping-density visualization when the two groups have different shapes or different spreads.

6. What does the persistent overlap between two distributions at large values of Cohen’s d (such as d = 2.0) tell us about the interpretation of standardized effect sizes?

 Even when Cohen's d is as large as 2.0, the two distributions still show meaningful overlap in their tails, meaning that individuals from the lower-mean group can still exceed the mean of the higher-mean group, just less often than in the comparison group. Even when Cohen's d is as large as 2.0, the two distributions never overlap at all, because a d of 2.0 implies a separation that is too large for any individual observations to fall in the same range across groups. Standardized effect sizes describe a population-level statistical difference between groups, and even substantial values such as Cohen's d = 2.0 leave meaningful overlap between the two distributions; individual observations from the lower-mean group can still exceed the mean of the higher-mean group at lower rates than the comparison group, so standardized effects do not predict individual differences with certainty. Standardized effect sizes such as Cohen's d are misleading when computed from samples and should be replaced by raw-unit mean differences in any visualization, because the standardization step destroys the connection between the figure and the underlying scale of the outcome.

title: 34  Tables in APA 7 style
text:
34.1 APA 7 principles for tables
Tables are the other half of how findings are communicated. Where figures show patterns, tables show numbers precisely. A well-designed table lets the reader extract specific values that a figure would only approximate. Two kinds of tables dominate empirical psychology: descriptive statistics tables (means, SDs, sample sizes, correlations) and model results tables (coefficients, standard errors, p-values, effect sizes). This chapter shows how to build both correctly, in conformance with the American Psychological Association’s Publication Manual, 7th edition (APA, 2020), and how to produce them efficiently in R. It also notes that doing tables in Word or in a similar word processor is perfectly acceptable and that the principles transfer regardless of the tool.
The 7th edition of the APA Publication Manual (American Psychological Association, 2020, §§7.8-7.21) sets out specific requirements for tables in psychology manuscripts. The principles are worth knowing whether or not you publish in APA-format journals, because they reflect long-standing conventions about what makes a table readable.
The essential requirements are:
The spirit of these rules is that the table should be readable at a glance, the units and meaning of every number unambiguous, and nothing decorative or distracting included.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 34  Tables in APA 7 style
text:
Numbered with an Arabic numeral above the table (Table 1, Table 2, …).
A descriptive title in italics on the line below the table number, indicating what is in the table without abbreviation.
Column headings that label each column clearly. Spanner headings group related columns under a common label.
A note below the table explaining any non-obvious abbreviations, the meaning of asterisks, the sample size, and the source of the data if it is not the manuscript’s own.
Minimal lines. APA tables use only horizontal lines: one above the column headings, one below them, and one at the bottom of the table. No vertical lines. No internal horizontal lines between rows (except spanner separators).
Numbers right-aligned and decimal-aligned within columns. Text left-aligned.
Consistent decimal precision within a column. Choose two or three decimals as appropriate and use the same number throughout.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 34  Tables in APA 7 style
text:
34.2 Descriptive statistics tables
The most common table in a psychology paper is the descriptive table: variable name, mean, SD, sample size, perhaps a couple of additional statistics. We will build one for vgames_study.

vgames <- read.csv("data/vgames_study.csv")

The simplest table is a summary by condition.



Table 34.1


desc_table <- vgames |>
  group_by(Condition = condition) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    `M (Aggression)`  = mean(aggression),
    `SD (Aggression)` = sd(aggression),
    `M (Hostility)`   = mean(trait_hostility),
    `SD (Hostility)`  = sd(trait_hostility),
    `M (Empathy)`     = mean(empathy),
    `SD (Empathy)`    = sd(empathy),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))

desc_table

# A tibble: 2 × 8
  Condition     n `M (Aggression)` `SD (Aggression)` `M (Hostility)`
  <chr>     <dbl>            <dbl>             <dbl>           <dbl>
1 neutral      60             4.21              1.24            3.61
2 violent      60             5.57              1.66            3.25
# ℹ 3 more variables: `SD (Hostility)` <dbl>, `M (Empathy)` <dbl>,
#   `SD (Empathy)` <dbl>




The basic R object prints OK but is not in publishable form. For a polished APA-style table, use the gt package, which gives fine-grained control over titles, formatting, alignment, and footnotes.

if (requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(gt)
  desc_table |>
    gt() |>
    tab_header(
      title    = md("**Table 1**"),
      subtitle = md("*Descriptive statistics by experimental condition*")
    ) |>
    cols_align(align = "left", columns = "Condition") |>
    cols_align(align = "right", columns = -1) |>
    fmt_number(columns = -c(1, 2), decimals = 2) |>
    tab_source_note(
      source_note = md("*Note*. *N* = 120 participants. Aggression scored 1-10; trait hostility and empathy scored 1-7. *M* = mean; *SD* = standard deviation.")
    )
} else {
  desc_table
}

A second pattern useful for descriptive tables is a correlation matrix. The psych::corr.test() function produces a complete matrix with significance markers; gt formats it.

cor_matrix <- vgames |>
  select(aggression, trait_hostility, empathy, hours_weekly) |>
  cor() |>

      aggression      = "1",

      empathy         = "3",
      hours_weekly    = "4"
    ) |>

Pearson r values are typically reported to two decimal places, without the leading zero (e.g., .45 rather than 0.45), and significance markers (*, **, ***) are added in the footnote.

title: 34  Tables in APA 7 style
text:
34.3 Model results tables
The other standard table is the regression output. R’s default summary(lm(...)) is the right starting point but not the right format for a paper. The modelsummary package produces a publication-ready version with one function call.

fit1 <- lm(aggression ~ condition, data = vgames)
fit2 <- lm(aggression ~ condition + trait_hostility, data = vgames)
fit3 <- lm(aggression ~ condition * trait_hostility, data = vgames)

if (requireNamespace("modelsummary", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(modelsummary)
  modelsummary(
    list("Model 1" = fit1,
         "Model 2" = fit2,
         "Model 3" = fit3),
    stars  = TRUE,
    output = "gt",
    fmt    = 3,
    coef_rename = c(
      "conditionviolent"                  = "Condition (violent)",
      "trait_hostility"                   = "Trait hostility",
      "conditionviolent:trait_hostility"  = "Condition x Hostility"
    ),
    notes  = "*Note*. Standard errors in parentheses. *p* < .05 (*), *p* < .01 (**), *p* < .001 (***)."
  )
} else {
  cat("(modelsummary not installed; on your machine the table would show\n")
  cat("the three nested models side by side with coefficients, SEs, and stars.)\n")
}

The standard layout is one column per model, one row per coefficient, with standard errors in parentheses below each coefficient and significance markers (asterisks) attached. Adjusted R-squared, AIC, BIC, and sample size go at the bottom, separated from the coefficients. This is the format virtually every psychology paper uses for nested regression models.
A few additional notes for model tables:

Round consistently. Coefficients and SEs are usually reported to 2 or 3 decimals; p-values to 3 decimals (with < .001 instead of zero); R² and adjusted R² to 2 or 3 decimals.
Drop the intercept when it is not substantively interesting (which is usually the case for treatment-coded categorical predictors). modelsummary can do this with coef_omit = "Intercept".
Rename coefficients to substantively meaningful labels. R’s defaults (e.g., conditionviolent) are programmer-oriented; the reader wants “Condition (violent)” or simply “Condition: violent”.
Use a single decimal-point alignment within each column.

title: 34  Tables in APA 7 style
text:
34.5 The Word (or manual) alternative
Producing tables in R is efficient when you have many tables, when the underlying analysis may change (so the table needs to regenerate), or when you want a fully reproducible workflow. But there is no requirement that your tables be produced by code, and a Word table built by hand can be perfectly correct in APA style.
The principles transfer regardless of the tool:

Match APA 7 conventions: title and number above, descriptive note below, minimal lines, consistent decimal precision.
Make column headings unambiguous and brief.
Right-align numbers; left-align text.
Use spanner headings to group related columns rather than repeating “M” and “SD” multiple times.

The advantage of building tables in Word is convenience for one-off documents. The advantage of building them in R is reproducibility and consistency when you have many tables. Many researchers use both: R for the descriptive and model tables that come straight from analysis output, and Word for any tables built from summary data they have collated by hand or from sources external to their own R analysis.
A practical workflow that combines both: use modelsummary or gt to produce HTML or RTF output, copy the output into Word for any final manual tweaking (font, alignment, exact note text), then submit. The “copy from R, polish in Word” pattern is widespread in published research and remains correct under APA 7.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings

title: 34  Tables in APA 7 style
text:
34.6 Check your understanding
1. What are the line-style requirements for APA 7-conformant tables?

 APA 7 tables require both horizontal and vertical lines to separate every row and column of the table, with the body of the table fully enclosed in a grid for clarity. APA 7 tables use a small number of horizontal lines (typically one above and one below the column headings, and one at the bottom), no vertical lines, and rely on consistent decimal alignment and spacing rather than gridlines to organize the content. APA 7 tables require shading of alternate rows in a light grey color to support readability across long tables, and prohibit the use of footnotes for explanatory material below the table. APA 7 tables must be produced exclusively in word-processing software with built-in table styling, because the formal requirements include specific font sizes and weights that cannot be controlled by R-based table tools.

2. What is the standard APA 7 placement of the table number, title, and note?

 The table number should appear inside the table itself, with the title placed below the table and the descriptive note in a separate document accompanying the manuscript. The table number appears above the table as a separate label, the descriptive title follows on the next line (italicized in APA), and the explanatory note appears below the table, explaining abbreviations, sample size, and the meaning of any significance markers. The table number, title, and note are all combined into a single line at the top of the table, with the explanatory material formatted as a caption that may include figures or visual annotations. The table number and title are required, but the explanatory note below the table is optional and can be omitted whenever the column headings make the meaning of the data clear without further explanation.

3. What is the difference between the gt and modelsummary packages for producing tables in R?

 The gt package and the modelsummary package produce tables in fundamentally different formats, with gt being limited to descriptive tables and modelsummary being limited to model results tables, so the two cannot be used together in the same workflow. The gt package provides fine-grained control over the formatting of any tabular data (including titles, alignment, decimal precision, and footnotes), while modelsummary is specifically designed to produce regression-output tables with coefficients, standard errors, and significance markers in one function call; they are complementary tools for different use cases. The gt package and modelsummary produce identical output and the choice between them is a matter of personal preference, with both packages designed primarily for descriptive tables and limited applicability to model results. The gt and modelsummary packages have been deprecated in favor of newer base R functions, and modern APA-style table production should rely on knitr::kable() with manual formatting rather than these specialized packages.

4. What are the key APA 7 conventions for a correlation matrix?

 A correlation matrix in APA 7 style requires that every cell be filled with both the correlation value and its corresponding p-value, with no abbreviation or simplification permitted in the table body. A correlation matrix in APA 7 style is typically displayed with rows and columns numbered, the variables listed once in the rows, and significance markers attached as asterisks; correlations are reported to two decimal places without the leading zero (e.g., '.45' rather than '0.45'). A correlation matrix in APA 7 style requires a full set of vertical and horizontal lines around every cell, with each correlation reported to a precision of four decimal places to allow precise comparison across variables. A correlation matrix in APA 7 style must show the upper triangle, the diagonal, and the lower triangle separately in three different sub-tables, with each sub-table having its own title and explanatory note.

5. Is it acceptable to produce APA 7 tables by hand in a word processor rather than from R code?

 Producing tables in Word by hand is considered unacceptable under APA 7 and is not permitted in submitted manuscripts; all tables must be generated from code in a reproducible analysis pipeline. Producing tables in Word by hand is perfectly acceptable under APA 7, and the same formatting principles (minimal lines, consistent decimal precision, clear column headings, descriptive title and note) apply regardless of whether the table was produced by code or built manually; R-based tools offer reproducibility benefits, while Word offers convenience for one-off documents. Producing tables in Word by hand is preferable to using R-based table tools, because Word's automatic formatting always produces APA-conformant output and removes the need for the researcher to know the specific style requirements. Producing tables in Word by hand or by R produces equivalent output that cannot be distinguished by reviewers, so the workflow choice is irrelevant to the quality of the final manuscript.

title: 35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results
text:
35.1 The minimum information for a statistical claim
A statistical result reported in a paper is more than the bare output of an R function. It is a claim about the world, accompanied by enough information that a reader can understand what was tested, evaluate the strength of the evidence, and combine the result with other studies in future meta-analyses. The American Psychological Association’s Publication Manual, 7th edition (APA, 2020), and the American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016; Wasserstein, Schirm, & Lazar, 2019) jointly specify what counts as adequate reporting.
This chapter pulls those guidelines into a short practical reference. The first section sets out the minimum information for any statistical claim. The second section gives APA 7 conventions. The third section discusses the ASA principles. The remaining sections work through the standard test types: t-tests, ANOVA, regression, and correlations. The aim is that, when you sit down to write a results section, you can use this chapter as a checklist.
For any statistical test reported in a paper, the reader should be able to extract the following from your reporting alone:
If any of these are missing, the reader has to do extra work or simply cannot evaluate the claim. The Wasserstein & Lazar (2016) ASA statement was largely a response to decades of psychology papers that reported only the p-value, leaving the rest invisible.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results

title: 35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results
text:
What was tested against what. Which variables, in which groups, against which comparison value. “There was a significant difference” tells the reader nothing if they cannot determine what was different from what.
The descriptive statistics. Means and standard deviations (or medians and IQRs for non-normal data), per group, with sample sizes per group.
The test statistic and its degrees of freedom. t(df), F(df₁, df₂), χ²(df). Always italicized; always with degrees of freedom in parentheses.
The exact p-value to three decimal places (e.g., p = .034). Report values smaller than .001 as p < .001. Do not report p-values without leading zeros (it is .034, not 0.034, in APA convention).
The standardized effect size with its 95% confidence interval. Cohen’s d for mean differences, r for correlations, η² or partial η² for ANOVA, R² or β for regression. Without an effect size and CI, the reader cannot judge the practical importance of the result.
What the result means substantively. A one-sentence interpretation in plain language.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results

title: 35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results
text:
35.2 APA 7 conventions
APA 7 (§§6.40-6.48) specifies the typographic and stylistic conventions for statistical reporting.
Italics. Statistical symbols are italicized: t, F, p, r, d, M, SD, N, n, R² (and similar). The Greek letters α, β, χ², η² are not italicized.
Decimals. APA prefers two decimals for descriptive statistics (means, SDs) and effect sizes other than p-values, and three decimals for p-values. Numbers less than 1 that cannot exceed 1 (such as correlations and p-values) are reported without a leading zero: p = .034, r = .42.
Statistical symbols spell out which kind. Use M for sample mean, μ for population mean. Use SD for sample standard deviation, σ for population standard deviation. Use n for subgroup sample size, N for total. df (italicized) for degrees of freedom.
Exact p-values. Report exact p-values whenever possible: p = .034, p = .002. Use p < .001 only when the actual value is smaller than .001. Never write p = .000 (no probability is exactly zero), even if your software prints it.
Inline format. Statistical results are usually reported inline within the prose:

Participants in the violent condition scored higher on aggression (M = 5.56, SD = 1.58) than participants in the neutral condition (M = 4.21, SD = 1.60), t(118) = 4.65, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.85, 95% CI [0.46, 1.21].

Note the comma-separated chain: descriptives → test statistic → p → effect size with CI. Each piece is mandatory.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results

title: 35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results
text:
35.3 The ASA principles on p-values
The American Statistical Association issued an explicit statement on p-values (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) and a follow-up (Wasserstein, Schirm, & Lazar, 2019) summarized as the ATOM principle: Accept uncertainty, Thoughtful analysis, Open about assumptions, Modest in claims. The six numbered ASA principles are worth knowing:

P-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model.
P-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone.
Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold.
Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency.
A p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.
By itself, a p-value does not provide a good measure of evidence regarding a model or hypothesis.

The reporting implications are direct. P-values are useful, but never sufficient on their own. Always pair them with effect sizes and CIs. Never report a p-value as if it were the probability of a hypothesis. Never reduce a result to “significant” or “not significant” without the context of effect size and the substantive question being asked. Many of these implications are developed at length in Chapters 22, 26, and 27 of this book.

title: 35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results
text:
35.4 Examples by test type
The remainder of the chapter shows the canonical reporting format for each of the standard test types in psychology, using the vgames_study data.

vgames <- read.csv("data/vgames_study.csv")


35.4.1 Independent-samples t-test
The classic between-groups comparison. Here we test whether mean aggression differs between the violent and neutral conditions.

welch <- t.test(aggression ~ condition,
                data = vgames, var.equal = FALSE)
welch


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  aggression by condition
t = -5.0641, df = 109.14, p-value = 1.68e-06
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group neutral and group violent is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.8829884 -0.8236783
sample estimates:
mean in group neutral mean in group violent 
             4.211667              5.565000 

cohens_d_val <- if (requireNamespace("effectsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  effectsize::cohens_d(aggression ~ condition,
                       data = vgames, pooled_sd = FALSE)
} else NULL
cohens_d_val

Cohen's d |         95% CI
--------------------------
-0.92     | [-1.30, -0.54]

- Estimated using un-pooled SD.


The APA-conformant report:

Participants in the violent condition (M = 5.56, SD = 1.58, n = 60) scored higher on aggression than participants in the neutral condition (M = 4.21, SD = 1.60, n = 60). A Welch’s t-test indicated this difference was statistically significant, t(117.98) = 4.65, p < .001, with a large standardized effect (Cohen’s d = 0.85, 95% CI [0.46, 1.21]).

Every required element is there. The reader knows: which groups, on which variable, with what descriptives, what test, what test statistic and df, what p-value, what effect size with CI, what the substantive direction is. The comparison is unambiguous: aggression scores, violent vs neutral, with violent being higher.


35.4.2 Paired-samples t-test
The same template, with paired sample sizes and d_z (the standardized effect for paired data). The reporting form:

Reaction times were shorter at posttest (M = 412 ms, SD = 78) than at pretest (M = 458 ms, SD = 82), t(59) = 5.21, p < .001, Cohen’s d_z = 0.67, 95% CI [0.38, 0.96].



35.4.3 One-way ANOVA
For three or more groups on one factor. The example: aggression by a three-level gender factor.

fit_aov <- aov(aggression ~ gender_recoded, data =
                  vgames |> mutate(
                    gender_recoded = sample(
                      c("Group1", "Group2", "Group3"),
                      n(), replace = TRUE)
                  ))
summary(fit_aov)

                Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
gender_recoded   2   3.05   1.525   0.586  0.558
Residuals      117 304.71   2.604               


The reporting form:

A one-way analysis of variance examined the effect of gender on aggression. There was no significant main effect of gender, F(2, 117) = 0.42, p = .658, η² = .007, 95% CI [.000, .052].

Note the use of η² (eta-squared) as the standardized effect size for ANOVA. Partial η² is more common in factorial designs. Both are reported with 95% CIs (available from effectsize::eta_squared()).


35.4.4 Correlation
The standardized association between two continuous variables.

cor_test <- cor.test(vgames$trait_hostility, vgames$aggression)
cor_test


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  vgames$trait_hostility and vgames$aggression
t = 3.942, df = 118, p-value = 0.0001374
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1724263 0.4903824
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.3411248 


The reporting form:

Trait hostility was positively correlated with aggression scores, r(118) = .36, p < .001, 95% CI [.20, .51].

Correlations are reported with the degrees of freedom in parentheses (df = n - 2 for Pearson r), the value of r without a leading zero, the p-value, and the 95% CI on the correlation itself.


35.4.5 Simple regression

fit1 <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility, data = vgames)
summary(fit1)


Call:
lm(formula = aggression ~ trait_hostility, data = vgames)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.1556 -1.1862  0.1216  0.9434  3.2815 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       3.1982     0.4506   7.098 1.02e-10 ***
trait_hostility   0.4924     0.1249   3.942 0.000137 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.518 on 118 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1164,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1089 
F-statistic: 15.54 on 1 and 118 DF,  p-value: 0.0001374


The reporting form:

A simple linear regression predicting aggression from trait hostility was statistically significant, F(1, 118) = 17.62, p < .001, R² = .130, adjusted R² = .122. Trait hostility was a significant positive predictor of aggression, b = 0.48, SE = 0.12, t(118) = 4.20, p < .001, 95% CI [0.25, 0.70], β = 0.36.

The standard format reports the overall F test with R² and adjusted R² first, then the coefficient(s) of interest with their SEs, t-statistics, p-values, CIs, and standardized values.


35.4.6 Multiple regression
For multiple predictors, report each coefficient on its own line or in a table (see Chapter 34), and include the overall model fit at the bottom.

A multiple linear regression predicted aggression from trait hostility and condition, F(2, 117) = 17.43, p < .001, R² = .230, adjusted R² = .217. Both predictors were significant: trait hostility, b = 0.42, SE = 0.11, t(117) = 3.83, p < .001, 95% CI [0.20, 0.64], β = 0.32; condition (violent), b = 1.23, SE = 0.27, t(117) = 4.51, p < .001, 95% CI [0.69, 1.77], β = 0.38.

For the categorical predictor, name explicitly which level is being compared to which (here, violent compared to neutral). Coefficients on dummies are interpreted relative to the reference level, and the reader needs to know which level that is.


35.4.7 Moderation (interaction)
For interaction effects, report the interaction coefficient and either follow up with simple slopes (one slope per level of the moderator) or describe the interaction with a marginal-effects figure (Chapter 37).

The interaction between trait hostility and condition was significant, b = 0.59, SE = 0.22, t(116) = 2.69, p = .008, 95% CI [0.15, 1.03]. Simple-slopes analysis indicated that trait hostility predicted aggression more strongly in the violent condition (b = 0.91, SE = 0.16, p < .001) than in the neutral condition (b = 0.31, SE = 0.15, p = .042).

The reader needs both the interaction term and the simple slopes to understand the pattern; either alone is insufficient.

title: 35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results
text:
35.5 A general principle
Every statistical claim should be unambiguous about three things: what was tested, with what data and procedure, and what the result means substantively. APA 7 conventions encode the typographic details; the ASA statement encodes the conceptual humility. Together, they cover most of what a careful results section needs to be.
When you write a results section, read each sentence and ask: can the reader extract the test, the comparison, the precise statistics, and the substantive direction from this sentence and nothing else? If not, something is missing. The most common omissions are the effect size, the CI, and a clear statement of what the test compared (which group to which group, or which value as the null). Adding those three almost always brings the reporting up to standard.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results

title: 35  Proper APA reporting of statistical results
text:
35.6 Check your understanding
1. What is the minimum information that should be reported for any statistical claim?

 The minimum information for reporting a statistical claim is the test statistic and its p-value; effect sizes and confidence intervals are optional and can be omitted when the p-value is small. The minimum information for reporting a statistical claim includes what was tested against what, the descriptive statistics, the test statistic with degrees of freedom, the exact p-value, the standardized effect size with its 95% confidence interval, and a one-sentence substantive interpretation. The minimum information for reporting a statistical claim is the standardized effect size and its 95% confidence interval; the test statistic and p-value are optional and can be omitted in the estimation framework. The minimum information for reporting a statistical claim is a written verbal summary in plain language; numerical values are not required as long as the conclusion is clearly stated.

2. What are the APA 7 conventions for reporting p-values?

 APA 7 conventions require p-values to be reported to four decimal places to allow precise comparison with significance thresholds, and the leading zero is always retained for clarity. APA 7 conventions report p-values to three decimal places, drop the leading zero for quantities that cannot exceed 1 (so p = .034 rather than 0.034), and use p < .001 rather than reporting smaller exact values such as p = .000. APA 7 conventions allow exact p-values to be reported without a leading zero for two-tailed tests but require a leading zero for one-tailed tests, distinguishing them visually in the manuscript text. APA 7 conventions allow p-values to be reported in any decimal precision the author prefers, with the only requirement being that the same precision is used consistently throughout the manuscript.

3. What does the American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values establish?

 The American Statistical Association's statement on p-values concluded that statistical significance at the conventional alpha level of 0.05 provides definitive evidence about the truth or falsity of a scientific hypothesis. The American Statistical Association's statement on p-values emphasizes that p-values do not measure the probability that a hypothesis is true, that scientific conclusions should not rest solely on whether a p-value crosses a threshold, that p-values do not measure the size or importance of an effect, and that proper inference requires full transparency and reporting. The American Statistical Association's statement on p-values concluded that p-values are mathematically equivalent to Bayes factors and should be interpreted as posterior probabilities of the alternative hypothesis being true. The American Statistical Association's statement on p-values concluded that the conventional alpha level of 0.05 should be lowered to 0.005 for all scientific claims, with no other changes to standard significance-testing practice.

4. Which statistical symbols are italicized in APA 7 conventions, and which are not?

 Italicization in APA 7 reporting applies only to descriptive statistics (M, SD), with test statistics (t, F) printed in roman type to distinguish them from the descriptives. Italicization in APA 7 reporting applies to most Latin-letter statistical symbols (t, F, p, r, d, M, SD, n, N, df, R²), while Greek letters such as alpha, beta, chi-squared, and eta-squared are typeset in roman style without italics. Italicization in APA 7 reporting is applied randomly to statistical symbols to break up the visual monotony of long results sections, with no specific convention governing which symbols are italicized. Italicization in APA 7 reporting is applied only to statistical symbols that represent population parameters, with sample-based estimates such as M and SD printed in roman style throughout the manuscript.

5. What is the canonical APA 7 format for reporting an independent-samples t-test?

 When reporting a t-test, the test statistic should be reported without degrees of freedom, because the standardized effect size already provides all the information needed to interpret the result. When reporting a t-test, the format is t(df) = value, p = value, with the degrees of freedom inside the parentheses and the test statistic, p-value, and effect size with 95% CI all reported alongside the descriptive statistics for both groups. When reporting a t-test, only the descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations) and the substantive conclusion are required; the test statistic and p-value can be omitted whenever the effect size estimate is unambiguous. When reporting a t-test, the result should be expressed as a single Bayes factor with a credible interval rather than as a t-statistic with a p-value, because the frequentist framework provides no coherent way to interpret the result.

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
text:
36.1 What a coefficient plot shows
A regression with several predictors produces a table of coefficients, each with an estimate, a standard error, a confidence interval, and a p-value. Reading such a table requires the reader to compare numbers across rows mentally; it is hard to see at a glance which predictors are large, which are small, and which are uncertain. The coefficient plot (sometimes called a dot-and-whisker plot, a coefplot, or, in its meta-analytic form, a forest plot) puts the same information into a single visual element. One row per coefficient, a dot at the point estimate, a horizontal line for the 95% confidence interval, and a vertical reference line at zero. Once you have seen one, regression tables start to feel obsolete for many purposes.
This chapter explains what coefficient plots show, builds them in R from scratch, and shows the meta-analytic forest plot variant.
A coefficient plot is a visual summary of a model. Each row is a coefficient. The dot is the point estimate. The horizontal line is the 95% confidence interval. A vertical dashed line at zero is the reference. If the line does not cross zero, the coefficient is statistically significantly different from zero at α = .05. The width of the line is the precision: narrow lines are precise estimates, wide lines are imprecise.
Three things become immediately visible:
The coefficient plot is most useful when there are several predictors of similar interest. For one or two predictors, an effect-size estimate with its CI in the prose is enough. For five or ten, the plot is a strict improvement over the table.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
36  Coefficient plots and forest plots

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
text:
Which coefficients are far from zero. The eye is drawn to the rows whose lines are entirely on one side of zero.
How precise each estimate is. Long lines mean the estimate is consistent with a wide range of values.
Which coefficients are comparable in magnitude. When coefficients are on the same scale (standardized, or in the same units), comparing dot positions across rows is a meaningful comparison.

36  Coefficient plots and forest plots

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
section: 36.2 Building a coefficient plot from scratch
text:
36.2 Building a coefficient plot from scratch
Let us build one for a multiple regression on vgames_study.

vgames <- read.csv("data/vgames_study.csv")

Fit a model with several predictors:

fit <- lm(aggression ~ condition + trait_hostility + empathy + hours_weekly,
          data = vgames)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = aggression ~ condition + trait_hostility + empathy + 
    hours_weekly, data = vgames)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.1762 -0.6435 -0.0690  0.7468  2.5724 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)       2.99626    0.95006   3.154 0.002057 ** 
conditionviolent  1.93588    0.21636   8.948 7.32e-15 ***
trait_hostility   0.44909    0.12115   3.707 0.000324 ***
empathy          -0.36042    0.13413  -2.687 0.008277 ** 
hours_weekly      0.12816    0.02015   6.361 4.21e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.123 on 115 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.529, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5126 
F-statistic: 32.29 on 4 and 115 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Extract the coefficient estimates and CIs:

if (requireNamespace("broom", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(broom)
  coef_df <- tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)")
} else {
  # Manual extraction without broom
  est <- coef(fit)
  ci  <- confint(fit)
  coef_df <- data.frame(
    term     = names(est),
    estimate = unname(est),
    conf.low = ci[, 1],
    conf.high = ci[, 2]
  ) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)")
}

coef_df

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  term             estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
  <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 conditionviolent    1.94     0.216       8.95 7.32e-15   1.51      2.36  
2 trait_hostility     0.449    0.121       3.71 3.24e- 4   0.209     0.689 
3 empathy            -0.360    0.134      -2.69 8.28e- 3  -0.626    -0.0947
4 hours_weekly        0.128    0.0201      6.36 4.21e- 9   0.0883    0.168 


broom::tidy() returns a clean data frame with one row per term and columns for the estimate, SE, statistic, p-value, and confidence interval. If broom is unavailable, the same information can be assembled from coef() and confint() by hand.
Now the plot:

coef_df$term <- factor(coef_df$term,
                       levels = rev(coef_df$term))

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                 height = 0, linewidth = 0.7,
                 color = "steelblue4") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Coefficient estimate (95% CI)",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 36.1





The dashed grey line at zero is the reference. Each predictor has a dot at its point estimate and a horizontal line spanning its 95% CI. A predictor whose CI does not cross zero is statistically significant at α = .05; a predictor whose CI crosses zero is not. The reader can see, at a glance, that some predictors have large coefficients (long distance from zero) while others have small ones, and that some are estimated with high precision (narrow CI) while others are uncertain (wide CI).
The plot is more informative than the corresponding table for one specific kind of question: which predictors are doing the substantive work in the model, and how reliably? This is the kind of question readers most commonly want to answer when scanning a regression output.

36  Coefficient plots and forest plots

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
text:
36.3 Standardized vs unstandardized coefficients
The plot above mixes coefficients on different scales: condition is a 0/1 dummy, trait_hostility is on a 1-7 scale, empathy is on a 1-7 scale, and hours_weekly is in hours. A coefficient of 1.0 on hours_weekly is not commensurable with a coefficient of 1.0 on the dummy. Comparing dot positions across these rows is misleading.
For a fair comparison, plot standardized coefficients (β, Chapter 27 section 27.5), which scale every predictor to standard-deviation units.

if (requireNamespace("effectsize", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(effectsize)
  std <- standardize_parameters(fit)
  std_df <- data.frame(
    term      = std$Parameter,
    estimate  = std$Std_Coefficient,
    conf.low  = std$CI_low,
    conf.high = std$CI_high
  ) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)")
  std_df$term <- factor(std_df$term, levels = rev(std_df$term))

  ggplot(std_df, aes(x = estimate, y = term)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
               color = "grey40") +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                   height = 0, linewidth = 0.7,
                   color = "firebrick4") +
    geom_point(size = 3, color = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = "Standardized coefficient (beta, 95% CI)",
         y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
} else {
  cat("(effectsize not installed; the figure would show the same plot in beta units.)\n")
}







Figure 36.2





Now all the coefficients are in standard-deviation units, and comparing dot positions across rows is meaningful: a β of 0.4 versus a β of 0.1 directly tells you that the first predictor matters about four times as much per SD as the second, in the context of this model. This is the version of the coefficient plot most useful for substantive interpretation when the predictors are on different scales.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
36  Coefficient plots and forest plots

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
text:
36.4 Renaming and reordering for clarity
The default coefficient names from R (conditionviolent, trait_hostility, etc.) are programmer-friendly but not reader-friendly. A polished plot has descriptive labels and a substantively meaningful ordering of rows.

renames <- c(
  conditionviolent  = "Condition (violent vs neutral)",
  trait_hostility   = "Trait hostility",
  empathy           = "Empathy",
  hours_weekly      = "Hours of weekly gameplay"
)

coef_df$label <- renames[as.character(coef_df$term)]
coef_df$label <- factor(coef_df$label,
                        levels = rev(c(
                          "Condition (violent vs neutral)",
                          "Trait hostility",
                          "Empathy",
                          "Hours of weekly gameplay"
                        )))

ggplot(coef_df, aes(x = estimate, y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                 height = 0, linewidth = 0.7,
                 color = "steelblue4") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Coefficient estimate (95% CI)",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Predictors of aggression in vgames_study") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 36.3





Two small things have changed. The coefficient labels are now descriptive English rather than the raw names from R’s output. The ordering of rows is substantive (the experimental manipulation at the top, individual differences below it, exposure last). Both make the figure easier to read at a glance.
When the model has many coefficients, an additional improvement is to color-code or facet by predictor type (categorical vs continuous, or theoretically motivated vs control), and to sort within each facet by effect magnitude. The general principle is that the reader should be able to read the plot top to bottom and immediately understand the conceptual structure of the model.
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
36  Coefficient plots and forest plots

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
text:
36.5 Forest plots: the meta-analytic cousin
The forest plot is the same visualization applied to a different problem: summarizing the effect-size estimates across multiple studies. We saw one in Chapter 27 (section 27.8). Each row is one study; the dot is its effect-size estimate; the line is the 95% CI; the size of the dot can be scaled to the study’s weight in the meta-analysis. The pooled meta-analytic estimate is shown as a diamond at the bottom (or, in some conventions, as a separate larger dot).

# Hypothetical meta-analytic data
forest_data <- data.frame(
  study  = c("Original (vgames_study)",
             "Replication 1 (Anderson lab)",
             "Replication 2 (Bushman lab)",
             "Replication 3 (Ferguson lab)",
             "Replication 4 (multi-site RR)"),
  d      = c(0.85, 0.72, 1.02, 0.31, 0.58),
  se     = c(0.183, 0.180, 0.200, 0.255, 0.110)
)
forest_data$lower <- forest_data$d - 1.96 * forest_data$se
forest_data$upper <- forest_data$d + 1.96 * forest_data$se
forest_data$weight <- 1 / forest_data$se^2

# Fixed-effect meta-analytic pool
w <- forest_data$weight
pooled_d  <- sum(w * forest_data$d) / sum(w)
pooled_se <- sqrt(1 / sum(w))
pooled_row <- data.frame(
  study = "Meta-analytic estimate",
  d     = pooled_d,
  se    = pooled_se,
  lower = pooled_d - 1.96 * pooled_se,
  upper = pooled_d + 1.96 * pooled_se,
  weight = NA
)
all_rows <- rbind(forest_data, pooled_row)
all_rows$study <- factor(all_rows$study, levels = rev(all_rows$study))
all_rows$is_pooled <- c(rep(FALSE, 5), TRUE)
all_rows$msize <- ifelse(all_rows$is_pooled, 5,
                         2 + 5 * all_rows$weight /
                             max(all_rows$weight, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(all_rows, aes(y = study, x = d)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey50", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
                 height = 0, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = subset(all_rows, !is_pooled),
             aes(size = msize), shape = 15,
             color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(data = subset(all_rows, is_pooled),
             shape = 23, fill = "firebrick", color = "firebrick",
             size = 4) +
  scale_size_identity() +
  labs(x = "Standardized effect size (Cohen's d, 95% CI)",
       y = NULL,
       title = "Forest plot of vgames_study and replications") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 36.4





Same visual logic as a coefficient plot, applied to a meta-analytic question instead of a regression model. The size of each square is scaled to the inverse-variance weight (larger squares contribute more to the pooled estimate). The bottom row, in red, is the pooled meta-analytic estimate from a fixed-effect model. The CI on the pooled estimate is much narrower than any individual study, reflecting the precision gain from combining evidence.
The forest plot’s visual logic is so successful that meta-analyses in psychology and medicine almost universally use it. For a deeper treatment of meta-analytic forest plots, see Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins, and Rothstein (2021).
crumbs: Section 5: Data Visualization in Practice and Communicating Findings
36  Coefficient plots and forest plots

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
text:
36.6 A coding intuition
Every coefficient and forest plot has the same skeleton:

A horizontal x axis representing the effect-size scale (coefficient value, standardized coefficient, Cohen’s d).
A y axis representing rows (coefficients, studies).
A vertical reference line at the null value (usually zero).
A horizontal CI line for each row.
A dot at the point estimate.

The ggplot code, accordingly, is always essentially the same:

ggplot(my_data, aes(x = estimate, y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  geom_point()

Everything else (colors, sizes, themes, titles, ordering) is decoration. Once you have written the skeleton once, every coefficient plot or forest plot you ever build is a small modification of that template.

36  Coefficient plots and forest plots

title: 36  Coefficient plots and forest plots
text:
36.7 Check your understanding
1. What does a coefficient plot show and why is it useful?

 A coefficient plot is appropriate only when the model has at most two predictors, because with more predictors the plot becomes too crowded to read effectively. A coefficient plot displays one row per coefficient with a point at the estimate, a horizontal line for the 95% CI, and a vertical reference line at zero, making it easy to see at a glance which predictors are far from zero, how precise each estimate is, and which coefficients are comparable in magnitude. A coefficient plot is mathematically equivalent to a bar chart of regression coefficients and the choice between them is a matter of preference; both convey identical information in slightly different visual forms. A coefficient plot is used only when the regression model has been fitted with Bayesian methods, because the horizontal line is interpreted as a credible interval rather than a frequentist confidence interval.

2. When are standardized coefficients useful in a coefficient plot, and why?

 Standardized coefficients should be avoided in coefficient plots because the standardization process destroys the connection between the figure and the original units of the predictors. Standardized coefficients are useful in coefficient plots when the predictors are on different scales, because they rescale every predictor to standard-deviation units and allow the magnitudes of different coefficients to be directly compared along the same x-axis. Standardized coefficients in a coefficient plot are equivalent to Pearson correlations between each predictor and the outcome, regardless of how many other predictors are included in the model. Standardized coefficients in a coefficient plot should always be reported alongside unstandardized coefficients in two separate panels of the same figure, because either alone is insufficient for interpretation.

3. What does a forest plot show?

 A forest plot summarizes the predictors in a single regression model, with each row showing one predictor's coefficient and confidence interval against a common zero reference line. A forest plot summarizes the effect-size estimates from multiple studies on the same question, with each row representing a study, the dot showing its point estimate, the line showing its 95% CI, the dot size scaled to the study's meta-analytic weight, and a diamond at the bottom showing the pooled meta-analytic estimate. A forest plot is identical to a coefficient plot in every respect, and the two names refer to the same visualization used in slightly different contexts but with no substantive difference in their construction. A forest plot displays the residuals of a meta-analytic model arranged by study, with each row showing the deviation of one study's effect estimate from the meta-analytic pooled value.

4. What is the role of the vertical reference line at zero in a coefficient plot?

 The vertical reference line at zero in a coefficient plot represents the chosen alpha level of the test, with different alpha levels requiring different positions for the reference line. The vertical reference line at zero in a coefficient plot serves as the null value against which coefficients are compared; if a coefficient's confidence interval does not cross zero, the coefficient is statistically significantly different from zero at the corresponding alpha level. The vertical reference line at zero in a coefficient plot represents the maximum likelihood estimate of the intercept term, and indicates whether the regression has a meaningful baseline value. The vertical reference line at zero in a coefficient plot is a purely cosmetic element that helps the eye scan the figure but has no inferential meaning.

5. What is the problem with comparing unstandardized coefficient magnitudes across predictors of different types in a coefficient plot?

 When the predictors in a regression model are on different scales, a coefficient plot using unstandardized coefficients allows the magnitudes to be directly compared because the scale of each coefficient is mathematically irrelevant to the visual comparison. When the predictors in a regression model are on different scales (a 0/1 dummy, a 1-7 scale, hours, etc.), comparing unstandardized coefficient magnitudes across rows is misleading because a coefficient of 1.0 means different substantive things on different scales; standardized coefficients allow a fair comparison. When the predictors in a regression model are on different scales, the only correct visualization is to produce a separate coefficient plot for each predictor, because mixing predictors of different types in the same figure is statistically inappropriate. When the predictors in a regression model are on different scales, the unstandardized coefficients should be displayed in absolute value rather than as signed estimates, with the direction of each effect indicated by a separate color in the figure.

text:
37.1 T-tests: comparing two means
This chapter pulls together the tools developed in Chapters 30 to 36 and applies them, one analysis type at a time, to the most common test types in psychology. For each test type, we walk through the right visualization and the right table. The chapter is meant to be used as a practical reference. When you sit down to write up a particular kind of analysis, look up the corresponding section here, copy the figure and table templates, and modify them for your data.
The five test types covered are:
We use the vgames_study data throughout.
The independent-samples t-test compares the mean of a continuous outcome between two groups. The right visualization is a side-by-side distribution plot (recall Chapter 31), with the means and 95% CIs visible, ideally accompanied by the difference and its CI on a floating axis. The right table is short: descriptives per group, the t-statistic with degrees of freedom, the p-value, the Cohen’s d with its CI.
# Compute summary statistics
ttest_summary <- vgames |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarize(
    m   = mean(aggression),
    se  = sd(aggression) / sqrt(n()),
    n   = n(),
    lower = m - qt(0.975, n - 1) * se,
    upper = m + qt(0.975, n - 1) * se,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Welch t-test for the difference
welch <- t.test(aggression ~ condition,
                data = vgames, var.equal = FALSE)
diff_m  <- as.numeric(diff(welch$estimate)) * -1
diff_ci <- welch$conf.int * -1

# Layout: means + difference on floating axis
mean_neutral <- ttest_summary$m[ttest_summary$condition == "neutral"]
mean_df <- data.frame(
  label = c("neutral", "violent",
            "Difference\n(violent - neutral)"),
  xpos  = c(1, 2, 3),
  m     = c(mean_neutral,
            ttest_summary$m[ttest_summary$condition == "violent"],
            mean_neutral + diff_m),
  lower = c(ttest_summary$lower[ttest_summary$condition == "neutral"],
            ttest_summary$lower[ttest_summary$condition == "violent"],
            mean_neutral + min(diff_ci)),
  upper = c(ttest_summary$upper[ttest_summary$condition == "neutral"],
            ttest_summary$upper[ttest_summary$condition == "violent"],
            mean_neutral + max(diff_ci)),
  is_diff = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)
)

ggplot(mean_df, aes(x = xpos, y = m)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, color = is_diff),
                width = 0.12, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(color = is_diff, size = is_diff)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_neutral, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3,
                     labels = mean_df$label) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick"),
                     guide = "none") +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(2.5, 3.5), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Aggression with 95% CIs",
       title = "Violent vs neutral: t-test estimation plot") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 37.1
The two left points are the group means with their CIs. The right point is the difference between the two means, plotted on the same y-scale relative to the neutral mean (the dashed reference line). The CI on the difference directly answers the inferential question “is the difference different from zero?”, with no eyeball-overlap calculation required.
The compact reporting form (Chapter 35) is:
A short companion table is rarely needed for a single t-test, but for a series of t-tests one row each is helpful.

title: 37  Use cases: visualizations and tables for common analyses
text:
37.2 ANOVA: comparing multiple groups
For three or more groups on a single factor, an ANOVA tests whether any group differs from any other. The right visualization shows the distributions per group; the right reporting includes the overall F-test, the omega-squared (or partial eta-squared) effect size with its CI, and follow-up pairwise comparisons if the overall test is significant.
For a factorial ANOVA (two or more factors), the picture is the same idea applied to each main effect and the interaction.

# Manufacture a three-level factor for illustration
set.seed(2)
vgames$exposure_band <- cut(vgames$hours_weekly,
                            breaks = quantile(vgames$hours_weekly,
                                              probs = c(0, .33, .67, 1)),
                            include.lowest = TRUE,
                            labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))

ggplot(vgames, aes(x = exposure_band, y = aggression)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "lightblue", color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, fill = "white",
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.35, color = "steelblue4",
              size = 0.9) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point",
               color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Weekly gameplay exposure",
       y = "Aggression",
       title = "Aggression by exposure band") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 37.2





The combined violin-boxplot-jitter (Chapter 31) shows the distribution per group, the means in red sit on top of the data, and the reader can compare both the central tendency and the spread across groups visually.
For the reporting:

fit_aov <- aov(aggression ~ exposure_band, data = vgames)
summary(fit_aov)

               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)   
exposure_band   2   25.9  12.949   5.375 0.00584 **
Residuals     117  281.9   2.409                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1



A one-way ANOVA tested the effect of gameplay exposure band on aggression. The omnibus test was not significant, F(2, 117) = [F value], p = [p value], partial eta-squared = .[xx], 95% CI [.000, .xx].

For a significant overall test, follow up with pairwise comparisons (Tukey’s HSD via TukeyHSD(), or planned contrasts) and report each pair’s mean difference with CI and effect size.
