title: 37  Use cases: visualizations and tables for common analyses
text:
37.3 Simple regression
A simple regression with one continuous predictor is most naturally visualized as a scatter with the fitted line and confidence band (Chapter 31). The corresponding table is essentially the lm() summary in cleaned form.

fit_simple <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility, data = vgames)

ggplot(vgames, aes(x = trait_hostility, y = aggression)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              color = "firebrick", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(x = "Trait hostility (1-7)",
       y = "Aggression (1-10)",
       title = "Aggression as a function of trait hostility") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 37.3





The dots are the participants, the line is the predicted aggression at each level of trait hostility, the shaded band is the 95% CI on the prediction line (computed automatically by geom_smooth()). For the reader, this figure answers two questions at once: how strong is the linear association, and how precisely is it estimated?
The reporting:

A simple linear regression predicted aggression from trait hostility, F(1, 118) = [F value], p < .001, R² = [.xxx], adjusted R² = [.xxx]. Trait hostility was a significant positive predictor, b = [value], SE = [value], t(118) = [value], p < .001, 95% CI [low, high], beta = [value].

title: 37  Use cases: visualizations and tables for common analyses
text:
37.4 Multiple regression
For two or more predictors, the right table is a multi-column regression table (Chapter 34), and the right figure is the coefficient plot (Chapter 36). When two predictors are of substantive interest, a side-by-side coefficient plot for both standardized and unstandardized coefficients can be informative.

fit1 <- lm(aggression ~ condition, data = vgames)
fit2 <- lm(aggression ~ condition + trait_hostility, data = vgames)
fit3 <- lm(aggression ~ condition + trait_hostility + empathy +
                       hours_weekly, data = vgames)

if (requireNamespace("modelsummary", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(modelsummary)
  modelsummary(
    list("Condition only" = fit1,
         "+ Hostility" = fit2,
         "Full model" = fit3),
    stars = TRUE,
    output = "gt",
    fmt = 3,
    coef_rename = c(
      "conditionviolent" = "Condition (violent)",
      "trait_hostility"  = "Trait hostility",
      "empathy"          = "Empathy",
      "hours_weekly"     = "Hours weekly"
    ),
    notes = "*Note*. Standard errors in parentheses. *p* < .05 (*), *p* < .01 (**), *p* < .001 (***)."
  )
} else {
  cat("(modelsummary not installed; on your machine the table would show\n")
  cat("the three nested models side by side with coefficients, SEs, and stars.)\n")
}

title: 37  Use cases: visualizations and tables for common analyses
text:
37.5 Moderation and marginal plots
A moderation analysis tests whether the slope of one predictor depends on the value of another. When the moderator is categorical (as in condition × trait_hostility), the figure is two regression lines, one per moderator level. When the moderator is continuous, the figure shows the predicted relationship at several representative values of the moderator (typically the mean and ±1 SD).

ggplot(vgames, aes(x = trait_hostility, y = aggression,
                   color = condition)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("neutral" = "#377eb8",
                                "violent" = "#e41a1c"),
                     name = "Condition") +
  labs(x = "Trait hostility (1-7)",
       y = "Aggression (1-10)",
       title = "Moderation: hostility-aggression slope by condition") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 37.5





If the two slopes differ noticeably, the visual fingerprint of moderation (Chapter 18) is present: the lines are not parallel. If they were parallel, the relationship would be the same in both conditions and there would be no interaction.
For the reporting:

The interaction between trait hostility and condition was significant, b = [value], SE = [value], t(116) = [value], p = [value], 95% CI [low, high]. Simple-slopes analysis indicated that trait hostility predicted aggression more strongly in the violent condition (b = [value], SE = [value], p < .001) than in the neutral condition (b = [value], SE = [value], p = [value]).

For a continuous moderator, the equivalent figure shows the predicted line at several moderator values:

# Predict at low, mean, high empathy
mean_emp <- mean(vgames$empathy)
sd_emp   <- sd(vgames$empathy)

fit_mod <- lm(aggression ~ trait_hostility * empathy,
              data = vgames)

newdata <- expand.grid(
  trait_hostility = seq(1, 7, by = 0.1),
  empathy = c(mean_emp - sd_emp, mean_emp, mean_emp + sd_emp)
)
preds <- predict(fit_mod, newdata, interval = "confidence")
newdata$predicted <- preds[, "fit"]
newdata$lower     <- preds[, "lwr"]
newdata$upper     <- preds[, "upr"]
newdata$empathy_level <- factor(
  rep(c("Low (-1 SD)", "Mean", "High (+1 SD)"),
      each = nrow(newdata) / 3),
  levels = c("Low (-1 SD)", "Mean", "High (+1 SD)")
)

ggplot(newdata, aes(x = trait_hostility, y = predicted,
                    color = empathy_level, fill = empathy_level)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2,
              color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "grey40", "firebrick")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "grey40", "firebrick")) +
  labs(x = "Trait hostility (1-7)",
       y = "Predicted aggression (1-10)",
       color = "Empathy",
       fill  = "Empathy",
       title = "Marginal effect: hostility-aggression slope at three empathy levels") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())







Figure 37.6





The three lines show the predicted relationship between trait hostility and aggression at three representative levels of empathy. If the lines are parallel, there is no interaction; if they fan out or converge, there is a moderation effect, and the visual pattern shows in which direction the moderator changes the relationship. This kind of plot is sometimes called a marginal effects plot or a conditional effects plot and is the standard visualization for continuous moderation.

title: 37  Use cases: visualizations and tables for common analyses
text:
37.6 The general principle
Each analysis type has a natural visualization that puts the substantive answer directly in front of the reader. The natural visualization is rarely the bar chart with error bars. It is, depending on the analysis: an estimation plot with a floating difference axis (t-test), a combined violin-jitter-mean by group (ANOVA), a scatter with fitted line (simple regression), a coefficient plot (multiple regression), or a multi-line marginal effects plot (moderation). Each of these is built with the same ggplot2 grammar (Chapter 30) and stacks the same kinds of layers; the difference is which layers, in which order, are most appropriate to the analysis.
When you reach for a visualization, ask first what the substantive question is, then choose the figure that answers it most directly. The corresponding table (Chapter 34) and reporting style (Chapter 35) follow from there.

title: 37  Use cases: visualizations and tables for common analyses
text:
37.7 Check your understanding
1. What is the appropriate visualization for an independent-samples t-test?

 The right visualization for a t-test is a standard bar chart with error bars showing the means of the two groups, because this is the most familiar format for psychology readers. The right visualization for a t-test puts both group means with their CIs alongside the difference between means with its own CI on a floating axis, so the inferential question 'does the difference exclude zero?' is visible directly without requiring the reader to combine separate CIs. The right visualization for a t-test is the underlying t-distribution with the observed t-statistic marked, because this makes the long-run frequency interpretation of the p-value visually apparent. The right visualization for a t-test is a single point estimate of Cohen's d with its 95% CI, with no display of the underlying data because the standardized effect size carries all relevant information.

2. What is the appropriate visualization for a one-way ANOVA?

 The right visualization for a one-way ANOVA is a single bar chart showing the grand mean across all groups, because the omnibus F-test is asking about the average aggregation across groups rather than individual group means. The right visualization for a one-way ANOVA shows the distribution of the outcome variable per group (using violin, boxplot, jitter, or a combination), with group means and 95% CIs overlaid, supporting visual comparison of both central tendency and spread across groups. The right visualization for a one-way ANOVA is the F-distribution with the observed F-statistic marked, because this directly conveys the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis of no group differences. The right visualization for a one-way ANOVA is the residual-versus-fitted-value diagnostic plot, because ANOVA assumes equal variances and the diagnostic plot is the only way to evaluate this assumption.

3. What is the appropriate visualization for a simple regression with one continuous predictor?

 The right visualization for a simple regression is a histogram of the residuals, which shows whether the assumption of normally distributed residuals is met by the data. The right visualization for a simple regression is a scatterplot of the outcome against the predictor with the fitted regression line and its 95% CI band overlaid, conveying both the strength of the linear association and the precision of the estimate. The right visualization for a simple regression is a bar chart of the coefficient values, because the height of each bar makes the relative magnitudes of the predictors easy to compare. The right visualization for a simple regression is a Q-Q plot of the standardized residuals against theoretical quantiles, because this shows whether the data meet the assumptions of the regression.

4. What is the appropriate visualization for a multiple regression with several predictors of similar substantive interest?

 The right visualization for a multiple regression is a single scatter plot showing the outcome variable as a function of all predictors simultaneously, with each predictor encoded as a different color or shape of point in the same scatter. The right visualization for a multiple regression is a coefficient plot, showing one row per predictor with the estimate as a dot and the 95% CI as a horizontal line, with standardized coefficients used when predictors are on different scales to allow a fair comparison of effect magnitudes. The right visualization for a multiple regression is a heatmap of the correlation matrix among the predictors, because multicollinearity is the central concern in interpreting a multiple regression and visualizing it is the most important diagnostic. The right visualization for a multiple regression is a forest plot of the predictors with each predictor's confidence interval shown in a different color, since each predictor's effect is contingent on the values of the other predictors.

5. What is the appropriate visualization for a moderation (interaction) effect?

 The right visualization for a moderation effect with a categorical moderator is a side-by-side bar chart showing the mean of the outcome at each combination of the focal predictor and the moderator level. The right visualization for a moderation effect with a categorical moderator is one regression line per level of the moderator on the same axes, so non-parallel lines reveal the interaction; for a continuous moderator, the equivalent is the predicted line at several representative values (often mean and ±1 SD) of the moderator. The right visualization for a moderation effect is the F-statistic distribution for the interaction term, because the interaction's significance is the key inferential question and the distribution makes the long-run frequency interpretation visual. The right visualization for a moderation effect is a single regression line averaged across moderator levels, since the moderation effect represents a deviation from the average relationship that should be inspected separately as a residual diagnostic.

title: 38  Audience-targeted reporting: scientific vs lay communication
text:
38.1 Why audience matters
The same finding can be communicated to many different audiences. A statistician will want the precise model and the full set of statistics. A fellow psychologist will want effect sizes and confidence intervals in their own theoretical context. A clinician will want practical implications. A journalist will want a clear narrative. A member of the public will want to know what it means for them. Each of these is a legitimate audience, and each requires a different version of the same content.
This chapter is about how to make those translations without distorting the underlying finding. It develops three messages. First, the audience determines almost every choice you make about how to present the result. Second, simplification for lay audiences is not the same as omission; you can keep the substantive accuracy while making the presentation more accessible. Third, every translation involves trade-offs, and the most common failure modes (too technical for the lay reader, too superficial for the scientific reader) are easy to fall into.
The chapter has no live code. The principles apply regardless of the analysis tool. The examples use the vgames_study running example for continuity.
A finding has many facets. It has the model that produced it, the test statistics, the effect size and its CI, the substantive interpretation, the practical implications, the limitations, and the next questions it raises. Different audiences care about different combinations of these.
A scientific peer in your subfield knows your theoretical context, can read regression output fluently, and will want a complete picture: the design, the model, the statistics, the effect sizes with CIs, the alternative explanations, the limitations. A scientific peer outside your subfield needs more help with context but the same technical level. A clinician needs less of the model details and more of the practical implications. A journalist wants a clear, memorable claim. A funder wants the impact. A member of the public wants to know whether the finding affects their life.
The same data, the same analysis, the same conclusion can be communicated to all of these audiences. The choices about which details to foreground, which to background, and which to omit entirely are what separate one presentation from another. Picking the right combination for the audience you are addressing is itself a skill, and the rest of the chapter develops it.
A few prerequisites for any presentation, regardless of audience:
If any of these are missing, no amount of audience-tailoring fixes the underlying problem. The next sections take them as given and discuss how to translate.

The substantive direction of the finding is correct and unambiguous. (“Violent gameplay was associated with higher aggression scores” is correct; “violent gameplay causes aggression” overstates the design.)
The magnitude of the finding is conveyed somehow. A practically negligible effect should sound that way; a substantial effect should sound that way too.

title: 38  Audience-targeted reporting: scientific vs lay communication
section: 38.2 The scientific audience: what they need
text:
38.2 The scientific audience: what they need
A scientific peer wants enough information to evaluate the claim and to integrate it into a future meta-analysis. The standard format, developed at length in Chapter 35, requires:

The design (who, how many, what manipulation).
The descriptive statistics by group.
The test statistic and its degrees of freedom.
The exact p-value to three decimals.
The standardized effect size with its 95% confidence interval.
A figure that shows the substantive answer directly (Chapter 31).
A table when there are multiple statistics or models (Chapter 34).
Limitations and alternative explanations.

For the scientific audience, under-reporting is the more common mistake. A results section that gives only the p-value, or only the mean difference without an effect size and CI, makes the work harder to evaluate and limits its usefulness for meta-analytic synthesis. Over-reporting is rarely a problem; if anything, more methodological transparency is usually better.
The scientific audience’s report is structured around the test: what was tested, what was found, what it means in the framework of the field’s theoretical questions. The reader is assumed to be able to read regression output, interpret CIs, and place the finding in the literature.
An example of a scientific-audience paragraph on the vgames_study aggression finding:

Participants in the violent condition (M = 5.56, SD = 1.58, n = 60) scored higher on the aggression measure than those in the neutral condition (M = 4.21, SD = 1.60, n = 60). A Welch’s t-test indicated this difference was statistically significant, t(118) = 4.65, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.85, 95% CI [0.46, 1.21]. The standardized effect size is large by conventional benchmarks, though the wide CI (spanning from 0.46 to 1.21) is consistent with effects ranging from moderately large to very large. The effect is consistent with the broader literature on short-term laboratory measures of aggression following violent media exposure (Anderson et al., 2010), though it is acknowledged that long-term real-world consequences are less well-supported and that the effect did not interact with baseline trait hostility in this study.

Every essential element from Chapter 35 is present: descriptives, test, effect size with CI, substantive interpretation, connection to the broader literature, honest acknowledgment of the limits. This is what scientific reporting looks like when done well.

title: 38  Audience-targeted reporting: scientific vs lay communication
section: 38.3 The lay audience: what they need
text:
38.3 The lay audience: what they need
A member of the public, a journalist, or a policy maker has different needs. They typically do not want the t-statistic or the standardized effect size; they want to know what the finding means, in concrete terms that connect to their own experience. The challenge is to convey the same substantive direction and magnitude without using the technical machinery.
Three strategies are particularly useful.
Translate effect sizes into concrete differences. A Cohen’s d of 0.85 is meaningless to a non-statistician. But “participants in the violent condition rated their aggression on the 10-point scale at about 5.6 on average, while participants in the neutral condition rated theirs at about 4.2; the difference, about 1.3 points on the scale, is large enough to be visible at the individual level in many cases but not all” is meaningful. The original-units mean difference is far more digestible than the standardized effect size, even though both convey the same finding.
Use a probability-of-superiority interpretation. For Cohen’s d of 0.85, the probability that a random participant from the violent condition will score higher than a random participant from the neutral condition is about 72%. This is a meaningful claim for a non-statistician: it converts the effect size into a question about individual instances, which is closer to how people naturally think about differences between groups.
Acknowledge uncertainty in plain language. A 95% CI of [0.46, 1.21] cannot be reported as such. But “the data are consistent with the effect being moderately large or quite large; we cannot say precisely how large without more studies” captures the uncertainty without the jargon. The phrase “the data are consistent with” is the most useful lay translation of a confidence interval; it conveys the range of plausible values without invoking the formal procedure.
A lay-audience version of the same vgames_study finding:

In our study, people who played a violent video game in the lab gave higher aggression ratings afterwards than people who played a neutral game. On the 1-to-10 aggression scale we used, the violent-game group rated themselves at about 5.6 on average, while the neutral-game group rated themselves at about 4.2; a difference of just over one point on the scale. This is a meaningful difference. Roughly, if we picked one person at random from each group, the violent-game person would score higher about 7 out of 10 times. The data are consistent with the effect being moderately large or quite large. This study, like other short-term lab studies, tells us about immediate effects in a controlled setting; it does not directly tell us about long-term real-world consequences, which would require a different kind of study to demonstrate.

The same finding, the same direction, the same magnitude, the same honest uncertainty, but without a single statistic that a non-statistician would not recognize. The substantive content is preserved; the technical apparatus is replaced with plain-language equivalents.

title: 38  Audience-targeted reporting: scientific vs lay communication
text:
38.4 Strategies for simplification without distortion
The hardest part of lay communication is keeping the simplification honest. Several patterns are common pitfalls:
Dropping uncertainty entirely. “The violent-game group was more aggressive than the neutral-game group” is technically correct but conveys a degree of certainty the data do not warrant. Adding “in this study” or “on average” or “the data are consistent with a meaningful difference” preserves the substantive claim while keeping the inferential modesty.
Overstating the design. A laboratory study with self-reported aggression measures says something specific about laboratory contexts and self-reports; it does not establish that violent gameplay causes long-term aggressive behavior in everyday life. Lay reporting should respect what the design can and cannot show, even when the audience would prefer a stronger claim.
Conflating significance with importance. “The result was statistically significant” tells a lay reader nothing about the magnitude; “the effect was large enough to matter at the individual level” tells them what they wanted to know. Convert the inferential statement into a substantive one.
Dropping the effect size in favor of “significant” / “not significant”. The lay version of the result should not be “we found a significant effect”; it should describe the effect’s size in original units or via probability-of-superiority. Significance language outside of the scientific context misleads.
Overusing analogies. A good analogy clarifies; a bad one introduces an unrelated mental model that distorts the finding. The probability-of-superiority interpretation is a good analogy because it preserves the statistical structure. Comparing a Cohen’s d to the height difference between men and women is also good (we used it in Chapter 27). Comparing an effect size to “the difference between night and day” or “earth-shattering” is bad.
The general principle: keep the substantive claim, the direction, the magnitude, and the uncertainty intact. Replace the technical vocabulary with plain-language equivalents. If you cannot translate without losing one of these, the simplification has gone too far, and the substantive claim needs to be qualified.

title: 38  Audience-targeted reporting: scientific vs lay communication
text:
38.5 A side-by-side example
The same finding, three audiences:
Scientific peer (full results paragraph).

Participants in the violent condition (M = 5.56, SD = 1.58, n = 60) scored higher on the aggression measure than those in the neutral condition (M = 4.21, SD = 1.60, n = 60). The difference was statistically significant, t(118) = 4.65, p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.85, 95% CI [0.46, 1.21]. The wide confidence interval suggests the effect could be moderately large or quite large; the precise magnitude is not pinned down by this single study. The result is consistent with short-term laboratory effects documented in prior literature, while the long-term and real-world implications remain an open question.

Clinician or applied audience.

People who played a violent video game showed higher self-reported aggression immediately afterwards than people who played a neutral game. The difference, about 1.3 points on a 10-point scale, is meaningful: roughly speaking, after the violent game, a randomly picked participant was more aggressive than a randomly picked participant in the control group about 70% of the time. The effect was observed in a short laboratory session and refers to immediate post-game ratings, not to longer-term changes in everyday behavior. Whether the effect carries practical consequences in real-world settings depends on additional research that this study does not provide.

Lay audience (general public, journalism).

People who played a violent video game rated themselves as more aggressive right afterwards than people who played a neutral game. The difference was about one point on a 10-point scale, which is enough to be noticeable in many individuals but not in all. The effect was clear within this study; how it translates to long-term real-world behavior outside the lab is a separate question that this study cannot answer.

The substantive content is identical across the three versions. What changes is the level of statistical detail, the vocabulary, and the framing. The scientific version foregrounds the technical machinery; the clinical version foregrounds the practical implication and the limits; the lay version drops the machinery entirely while keeping the direction, magnitude, and honest acknowledgment of the design’s limits.
A practical exercise: take any recent finding you have written about in scientific language, and try to produce the clinical and lay versions. Compare what you had to change and what you had to keep. The skill of audience translation is built almost entirely by practice.

title: 38  Audience-targeted reporting: scientific vs lay communication
text:
38.6 A general principle
Every translation involves a trade-off. The scientific version is precise but unreadable to a non-specialist. The lay version is accessible but lacks the technical depth. Neither is the “right” version; they are different versions for different purposes. The most important habit is to choose deliberately, write the version your audience needs, and avoid the failure mode of using the wrong version for the wrong audience (a scientific paragraph in a press release, or a lay summary in a methods section).
For most researchers, most of the time, the scientific version is the default and the lay version is the translation. The discipline of the lay version is good for the scientific version, too: a researcher who can explain their finding to a non-specialist tends to also be able to write a clearer scientific results section, because the act of translating forces them to identify what the finding actually is, separately from the technical apparatus that produced it.
Section 5 closes here. The chapters in this section together cover the visual and verbal communication of statistical findings: the principles of ggplot2 (Chapter 30), visualizations for means and conditional means (Chapter 31), count data (Chapter 32), distributions (Chapter 33), APA tables (Chapter 34) and reporting (Chapter 35), coefficient and forest plots (Chapter 36), use cases by analysis type (Chapter 37), and audience-targeted communication (this chapter). Together with the statistical content of Sections 3 and 4, they cover the full pipeline from collecting data to communicating findings to the audience that needs to hear them.

title: 38  Audience-targeted reporting: scientific vs lay communication
text:
38.7 Check your understanding
1. How should the same statistical finding be presented to different audiences?

 The same statistical finding should be reported in identical language regardless of the audience, because changing the wording for different audiences introduces ambiguity and is incompatible with reproducible science. The same statistical finding should be presented at different levels of technical detail depending on the audience, with the substantive direction, magnitude, and uncertainty preserved across versions but the vocabulary and framing adapted to what the audience can interpret and use. The same statistical finding should be reported in technical language only when communicating with other researchers in the same subfield, and in lay language for all other audiences including clinicians, who do not require statistical detail in their professional practice. The same statistical finding should be presented in the most technical version possible for all audiences, because simplification distorts the underlying claim and is incompatible with honest scientific communication.

2. What does a scientific reporting paragraph require?

 A scientific reporting paragraph requires only the p-value of the statistical test, because the p-value carries all the information about both the effect size and the direction of the result in a single number. A scientific reporting paragraph requires the design, descriptive statistics by group, test statistic with degrees of freedom, exact p-value, standardized effect size with 95% CI, substantive interpretation, and acknowledgment of limitations, so that peers can evaluate the claim and integrate the result into future meta-analyses. A scientific reporting paragraph requires only the standardized effect size and its confidence interval, with the test statistic and p-value being optional under the new statistics framework which considers these legacy reporting conventions. A scientific reporting paragraph requires a verbal description of the substantive direction and magnitude without numerical statistics, because numerical reporting is the responsibility of any supplementary tables rather than the prose.

3. What strategies are most effective for translating an effect size to a lay audience?

 Translating an effect size for a lay audience requires converting the standardized effect to a percentage of variance explained, because this is the most intuitive quantity for non-statisticians to understand. Translating an effect size for a lay audience benefits from concrete reformulations such as the raw mean difference in original units, the probability of superiority (the chance that a random observation from one group exceeds one from another), and plain-language statements about the consistency of the data with a range of magnitudes. Translating an effect size for a lay audience requires reporting only the p-value, because lay readers are most familiar with the concept of statistical significance and any other quantity introduces unnecessary complexity. Translating an effect size for a lay audience requires using emphatic language such as 'dramatic' or 'enormous' to convey the importance of the finding, because lay readers respond more strongly to qualitative descriptions than to numerical claims.

4. What is the right way to simplify a finding for a lay audience without distorting it?

 Simplification for a lay audience requires omitting all mention of uncertainty, because non-statisticians cannot interpret confidence intervals or p-values and including them would only confuse the substantive claim. Simplification for a lay audience preserves the substantive claim, the direction, the magnitude, and the uncertainty intact while replacing the technical vocabulary with plain-language equivalents; failures of simplification include dropping uncertainty entirely, overstating the design, conflating significance with importance, and overusing analogies that distort the underlying finding. Simplification for a lay audience is best achieved by using extensive analogies to physical phenomena (such as comparing effect sizes to the height of buildings or the speed of light), because analogies are universally understood across audiences. Simplification for a lay audience is unnecessary because journalists and non-specialists should be expected to consult specialists when they encounter statistical claims they do not understand, rather than expecting researchers to adapt their communication.

5. What are the most common failure modes of audience-targeted reporting?

 The most common failure mode of audience-targeted reporting is using the lay version of a finding in a methods section, because methods sections require lay-accessible descriptions of the statistical procedures used. The most common failure modes of audience-targeted reporting are using the wrong version for the audience (a scientific paragraph in a press release, or a lay summary in a methods section), dropping uncertainty entirely in the lay version, and conflating statistical significance with practical importance in the public-facing version. The most common failure mode of audience-targeted reporting is using technical vocabulary in a lay version, because the substantive claim cannot be expressed accurately without technical terms. The most common failure mode of audience-targeted reporting is using too many decimal places in the numerical statistics of either the scientific or the lay version, because excessive precision implies a degree of certainty the underlying data do not warrant.

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
text:
39.1 The question many studies are really asking
Sections 3 and 4 of this book taught you how to fit a linear model and how to make a calibrated inferential claim about a coefficient. Section 5 taught you how to visualize and report the result. Across all of those chapters, the example you have returned to most often is the comparison between aggression scores in the violent and neutral conditions of vgames_study. In Chapter 17, when we introduced categorical predictors in regression, we fitted the simple model
The row labeled conditionviolent has an Estimate of approximately 1.35 aggression scale points, with a 95% confidence interval that excludes zero. We have used this number throughout the book.
The question this section asks is: what is that 1.35 actually telling us? More specifically: is it the causal effect of playing the violent video game on aggression? Or is it only an association, a difference in observed scores that has no particular causal meaning?
This is one of the most important questions a quantitative researcher can ask, and it is also the most commonly mishandled. The answer is not given by the data themselves, and it is not given by any statistical procedure. It depends on the design of the study and on the causal reasoning that links the data to the world. Section 6 is about that reasoning. This chapter is the motivation: why “data alone” cannot tell us which arrows in nature point which way.
In almost every published study you have ever read, the underlying question is some version of:
A new medication is tested for whether it causes blood pressure to drop. A teaching method is tested for whether it causes students to learn more. A randomized control trial of a vaccine asks whether the vaccine causes fewer infections. In vgames_study, the underlying question is whether playing the violent video game causes increased aggression.
Note the word “almost”. Not every research question is causal. Some studies are purely descriptive: they aim to characterize a population (how many young adults play violent games at all, what the distribution of trait hostility looks like in a community) without taking a stand on what causes what. Some studies are purely predictive: they aim to build a model that forecasts an outcome accurately (which patients will respond to a treatment, which students will drop out) without necessarily explaining why. Descriptive and predictive questions are entirely legitimate, and for many practical purposes they are the right questions. The framework developed in Section 6 is not needed if your goal is description or prediction. It is needed when your goal is causal: when you want to make a claim about what would change if we intervened.
When the question is causal (and it often is, especially in psychology, medicine, and policy), we need not just statistical association but the additional reasoning that licenses calling that association a cause. If we want to act on a finding, prescribe a drug, adopt a curriculum, run a public-health campaign, ban or permit a video game, we need to know not just that two variables are associated but that one causes the other. An association is descriptive: people who play violent games happen to be more aggressive in our sample. A causal claim is interventional: if you put someone in front of a violent game, their aggression will go up.
The uncomfortable truth, which Section 6 is built around, is that statistics by itself cannot answer the question “did X cause Y?” Statistics describes what is in the data. It tells you that two variables are correlated, that one group has a higher mean than another, that an effect is unlikely under the null hypothesis. None of that, on its own, licenses the causal conclusion. The bridge from “X and Y are associated” to “X caused Y” requires something more than statistics: it requires the right kind of design and the right kind of causal reasoning.

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
text: Did X cause Y?
crumbs: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
text:
39.2 The aspirin example
A simple example makes the point. Imagine you have a headache. You take an aspirin. Twenty minutes later, your headache is gone. Did the aspirin cause the relief?
You might think: obviously yes. But pause and consider what you would need to know to be sure. Your headache might have gone away on its own. You also drank a glass of water with the aspirin. You also lay down for a few minutes. You also stopped looking at the screen that may have been straining your eyes. The aspirin is one candidate explanation among several for why your headache went away.
To know that the aspirin specifically caused the relief, you would need to compare:

What happened. You took aspirin and your headache went away.
What would have happened otherwise. What your headache would have done if you had not taken aspirin (but had still drunk water, lain down, and stopped using the screen).

The second part is the tricky part. You cannot observe what would have happened otherwise, because you actually did take the aspirin. There is no version of the world where you simultaneously did and did not take it. This second thing, the thing that would have happened in the world where you made a different choice, is called the counterfactual (“contrary to fact”), and it is the missing ingredient that statistics by itself cannot give you.
The figure below depicts the structure of the counterfactual. The timeline starts on the left with a single shared history: you have a headache. At the decision point, the timeline forks. Down one branch (the factual branch we actually lived through), you took the aspirin and your headache improved. Down the other branch (the counterfactual branch we did not live through), you did not take the aspirin, and what happened to your headache is unknown. We never get to see down both branches at once.








Figure 39.1





Three features of the figure carry the central conceptual lesson. First, the two branches share a past: they both grow from the same single line. Counterfactuals are about the same person in what-if scenarios, not about two different people. Second, only one branch is solid (the factual branch we lived); the other is dashed (the counterfactual branch we did not live). The dashed branch is what we wish we knew but cannot directly observe. Third, the gap between the two endpoints (the double-headed arrow on the right) is the individual causal effect of the treatment. If the headache was going to clear up anyway, the gap is small. If the aspirin really did the work, the gap is large. We never directly see the gap, because we never see both endpoints for the same person.
The aspirin example is small and trivial. The same logic scales up to any study you have ever run.
crumbs: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
text:
39.3 The video game version
Apply the same logic to vgames_study. We see that participants in the violent condition scored higher on aggression than participants in the neutral condition. We computed the difference as approximately 1.35 aggression-scale points. We tested it, we plotted it, we discussed effect sizes for it.
Did the violent video game cause that 1.35-point difference?
To know, we would need to compare:

What happened. Participants in the violent condition had a mean aggression of about 5.56.
What would have happened otherwise. What the aggression mean would have been for those same participants if they had played the neutral game instead.

The second is the counterfactual, and we cannot observe it directly. We did not have the violent-condition participants also play the neutral game; we used different participants for each condition. The 1.35-point difference compares two groups, not one group under two conditions.
This is where things become delicate. The two groups will only give us a clean answer to the causal question if they are comparable in every relevant way except for the game they played. If they differ on any other dimension that also affects aggression (trait hostility, baseline mood, age, prior gaming experience), then part of the 1.35-point gap could be due to those other differences rather than to the game itself. The data alone do not tell us how to disentangle the two.
The figure below makes the worry concrete. The same observed group difference can arise from three completely different causal stories.








Figure 39.2





All three of these stories produce a positive association between game type and aggression scores. All three would show up in a cor() or t.test() or lm() output identically. The data cannot tell us which story is right because the data look the same regardless of where the arrows point.
Story 1 is what we usually want to claim: the violent game makes people more aggressive. Story 2 is the classic confound: trait-hostile people choose the violent game and tend to score higher on aggression measures, so the two are correlated even without the game doing anything. Story 3 is reverse causation: people who are already feeling more aggressive that day choose the violent game. Each story implies a different action in the world (if you ban the game, only Story 1 predicts that aggression will go down).
This is the heart of the matter. The same lm() output is compatible with three completely different causal stories, and statistics alone cannot tell us which story is the right one. The number 1.35 is the same in all three. The substantive meaning is different.
crumbs: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
section: 39.4 What statistics can and cannot do
text:
39.4 What statistics can and cannot do
The boundary is now precise. Statistics can do the following:

Tell us whether two variables are associated and, if so, how strongly.
Quantify our uncertainty about that association (standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values).
Fit a model that describes the data using a specific functional form.

Statistics cannot, by itself, do the following:

Tell us whether one variable causes another.
Distinguish among causal stories that produce the same observed associations.
Tell us what would have happened in a counterfactual world that was not observed.

The cannots are not failures of statistics. They are outside the domain of statistics. To answer them, we need a separate framework that lets us reason about causes, counterfactuals, and the structure of the world that generated the data. That framework is what this section is about.
We will see that there are essentially two routes from the data to a causal claim:

By design. If the treatment was randomly assigned, then the comparison of means is a causal estimate, because randomization rules out alternative causal stories at the level of the procedure. This is the route a randomized experiment takes.
By assumption. If randomization is not possible, we can sometimes recover the causal effect from observational data, but only by making explicit assumptions about which variables cause which others. Those assumptions are not derivable from the data; they come from theory, prior research, and domain knowledge.

Section 6 develops both routes. Chapter 40 introduces the formal framework (potential outcomes). Chapter 41 develops the randomization route. Chapters 42, 43, and 44 develop the by-assumption route, using DAGs to make assumptions visible and the backdoor criterion to tell us when those assumptions license a causal interpretation.
crumbs: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
section: 39.5 How this section connects to what you already know
text:
39.5 How this section connects to what you already know
You already have most of the technical machinery you need. The lm() syntax from Section 3 will return in every chapter of this section, unchanged. The standard errors, confidence intervals, and effect sizes from Section 4 still apply. The visualization tools from Section 5 will be used to draw DAGs and to communicate causal claims clearly.
What is new is the interpretation of what those tools produce. The same lm() output can carry a causal interpretation or a purely descriptive one, depending on the design and the reasoning behind it. The job of this section is to teach you to read the same number two different ways and to know which reading is appropriate when.
A more pointed way to put it: the same regression lm(aggression ~ condition) from Chapter 17 is the regression we will look at in Chapter 41 as a causal estimate. We will not change the code. We will not refit anything. What changes is what we are entitled to say about the coefficient. In Chapter 41, with random assignment, the 1.35-point coefficient is the average treatment effect: the causal increment in aggression caused by playing the violent game rather than the neutral game. Without random assignment, the same number is just a descriptive comparison of two groups that may or may not have been comparable to begin with.
This is the section’s main pedagogical move. The math does not change. The license to interpret it changes.
crumbs: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
text:
39.6 Roadmap
The remainder of Section 6 develops the framework step by step.

Chapter 40 introduces the potential outcomes framework: the formal way to think about counterfactuals. We will define Y(1) and Y(0), the two parallel universes in which a person is or is not treated, and we will state the fundamental problem of causal inference (we can only ever observe one of these per person). We will then introduce the average treatment effect (ATE) as the achievable target.
Chapter 41 develops randomization as the cleanest licensing mechanism. We will see why random assignment makes the treatment and control groups exchangeable, why this allows the comparison of group means to estimate the ATE, and how this licenses the regression coefficient we have already been computing in lm(aggression ~ condition). We will distinguish sampling uncertainty (the topic of Section 4) from causal uncertainty (the topic of this section) and notice that the two stack.
Chapter 42 introduces directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), the diagrammatic tool for drawing causal assumptions. We will see how nodes (variables) and arrows (causal claims) combine into paths and how those paths reveal which variables transmit causal effects and which transmit only spurious associations. The DAG is the central tool for the observational route to causal inference.
Chapter 43 develops the three classic third-variable roles: confounders, mediators, and colliders. Each has a distinctive structure in a DAG, each has a distinctive rule about whether to include it as a control, and each comes with a worked vgames_study example. The mirror-image relationship between confounders and colliders is the conceptual punchline of the chapter.
Chapter 44 states the backdoor criterion: the procedural rule that lets you choose the right control set given a DAG. We will discuss the Table 2 fallacy (the temptation to interpret every coefficient in a multiple regression as a causal effect) and close with the bigger message: statistical control requires causal justification. The mechanics of lm() do not change; what changes is what set of variables you put on the right-hand side and why.

What we will not develop in detail in Section 6 are the analytical methods that specifically aim to identify causal effects from observational data (propensity score methods, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, doubly robust estimation, etc.). These methods are built on top of the conceptual framework developed here, and they go beyond the scope of this book. Chapter 44 names them briefly and points to standard references where you can learn each of them in depth (Hernán & Robins, 2020; Imbens & Rubin, 2015; Chatton & Rohrer, 2024). Without the framework Section 6 builds, those methods can look like a grab bag of statistical tricks; with the framework in place, they become natural extensions of the same logic.
By the end of Section 6, you should be able to look at any quantitative claim in a paper and ask the right questions: was the treatment randomly assigned? If not, what causal structure does the author appear to be assuming? Are the right variables being controlled for, and the wrong ones left out? Is the headline claim a causal claim or only a descriptive one, and does the design support that reading?
The data we have used throughout this book have not changed. What this section adds is the framework for reading those same data causally, in addition to the descriptive and inferential readings we have already developed.

title: 39  Why data alone does not tell us causes
text:
39.7 Check your understanding
1. What is the relationship between statistical analysis and causal claims?

 Statistical analysis on a sample of data is sufficient to establish causal claims, because correlation coefficients and regression slopes directly measure causal effects whenever they reach statistical significance. Statistical analysis describes associations in the data but does not by itself license causal claims, because the same observed association can arise from several different causal structures (the cause directly producing the effect, a common cause producing both, reverse causation, etc.) and the data cannot distinguish among them. Statistical analysis cannot make causal claims under the frequentist framework but can under the Bayesian framework, because the Bayesian framework's use of prior information automatically rules out alternative causal explanations of the data. Statistical analysis can establish causal claims only when applied to non-normal data, because Gaussian approximations smooth over the kind of skewed distributions in which causal effects become detectable.

2. What is a counterfactual in the context of causal inference?

 A counterfactual is a hypothesis that the researcher rejects after observing the data, used in the frequentist framework to compute the long-run rejection rate of a statistical test. A counterfactual is a contrary-to-fact scenario describing what would have happened in a world where the cause of interest had taken a different value; it is the missing ingredient that ordinary statistical description cannot supply on its own. A counterfactual is a hypothetical sample of data drawn from a different population, used in meta-analysis to estimate the heterogeneity of effects across studies. A counterfactual is a regression coefficient computed from a transformed version of the outcome variable, designed to remove the influence of measurement error on the estimated effect.

3. Why does observing a regression coefficient or correlation not by itself license a causal claim?

 The same observed association between two variables can only arise from one specific causal structure, which can be identified by examining the shape of the joint distribution and the marginal distributions of the data. The same observed association between two variables can arise from several different causal structures (a direct cause, a common cause producing both, reverse causation, or various combinations), and the data alone cannot distinguish among them without additional assumptions or design features. The same observed association between two variables can arise from multiple causal structures, but the structures can always be distinguished by computing higher-order moments of the joint distribution such as the kurtosis or skew of the residuals. The same observed association between two variables always implies a direct causal relationship, because in a correctly specified statistical model alternative causal structures would produce systematically different correlations from the observed one.

4. What role does random assignment play in the interpretation of a regression coefficient?

 Random assignment of the treatment does not change the interpretation of a regression coefficient; the coefficient describes the same association regardless of how the treatment was delivered to participants. Random assignment of the treatment provides a design-based license for interpreting a regression coefficient causally, because randomization makes the treatment and control groups comparable on all other variables, so the difference in outcomes cannot be attributed to pre-existing differences between the groups. Random assignment of the treatment makes the regression coefficient mathematically larger than it would be without random assignment, by a factor that depends on the sample size and the alpha level chosen for the test. Random assignment of the treatment is required for the calculation of standard errors and p-values, because the frequentist sampling framework only applies when each participant has an equal probability of receiving each level of the treatment.

5. How does Section 6 of this book relate to the statistical tools developed in earlier sections?

 Section 6 of this book will replace the lm() function with specialized causal-inference functions, because regression cannot be used for causal claims and a separate set of tools is required for this purpose. Section 6 of this book will continue to use the lm() function and other tools introduced in Sections 3, 4, and 5, but will develop the additional reasoning required to interpret the output of these tools causally rather than merely descriptively; what changes is the interpretation, not the math. Section 6 of this book will use specialized graphical software to draw causal diagrams that cannot be produced in R, because the standard plotting tools in ggplot2 are not designed for the kind of network visualization required for causal inference. Section 6 of this book will treat causal inference as fundamentally Bayesian and will require the reader to abandon the frequentist tools developed in Sections 3 and 4 in favor of a fully Bayesian approach to estimation.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
text:
40.1 The two parallel universes
Chapter 39 ended with a problem. We want to know whether the violent video game caused the higher aggression scores we observed in vgames_study, but the data alone are compatible with multiple causal stories. To make progress, we need a more formal way to talk about what we mean by “cause,” precise enough that the framework will tell us exactly what we can and cannot learn from a given dataset.
This chapter develops that framework. It is called the potential outcomes framework, or the Rubin causal model, after Donald Rubin who developed it in a series of papers beginning in the 1970s (Rubin, 1974). The framework is built around two simple but powerful ideas: that every person has two potential outcomes (one for each treatment they might receive), and that we can only ever observe one of them. The chapter develops these ideas step by step, applies them to vgames_study, and introduces the average treatment effect as the quantity we will spend the rest of Section 6 learning to estimate.
The math in this chapter is light. The concepts are heavy. Take it slowly.
Let’s start with one participant from vgames_study. Call her Anna. Anna walks into the lab. The experimenter assigns her to play the violent game for fifteen minutes. Afterwards, Anna fills out the aggression questionnaire and scores 6 out of 10.
Did playing the violent game cause Anna’s aggression to be 6? To answer, we need to know what Anna’s aggression score would have been if she had played the neutral game instead. There are three possibilities:
The data we collected does not tell us which of these is true. We see Anna scored 6 after the violent game. We do not see what she would have scored after the neutral game. There is no version of the experiment where Anna simultaneously did and did not play the violent game.
The potential outcomes framework imagines this by means of the two parallel universes thought experiment. When Anna walks into the lab, the universe (in our minds) splits in two:
In Universe 1, Anna’s score is 6. In Universe 0, Anna’s score is 4. The difference, 6 − 4 = 2, is the individual causal effect of the violent game for Anna specifically. It is exactly what we want to know. And in this thought experiment, where both universes are visible, we can compute it directly.
The problem is that we live in one of these universes, not both. Anna actually played the violent game. We saw her score of 6. The value of her score in the unrealized universe (the neutral one) is something we have to infer somehow if we want to make a causal claim.
Figure 40.1
The blue bar is what we observed in our world. The grey bar is the counterfactual: it is what would have happened in the universe we did not see. The difference between them (the height of the arrow at the top of the figure) is the individual causal effect for Anna. The framework’s central problem is that we observe only one of the two bars per person, and so the difference is never directly computable.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
text:
Maybe it would have been 6 too. Then the violent game had no effect on Anna; she would have scored 6 regardless of which game she played, and the game was causally irrelevant.
Maybe it would have been 4. Then the violent game raised her aggression by 2 points. The game had a real causal effect on her of +2.
Maybe it would have been 8. Then the violent game actually calmed her down, lowering her aggression by 2 points. The game had a causal effect of −2.




Universe 1. Anna is assigned to play the violent game. Her aggression score in this universe is 6.
Universe 0. Anna is assigned to play the neutral game. Her aggression score in this universe is, say, 4.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
text:
40.2 The notation
Now we attach formal notation to this picture. The notation looks fancy but it just labels the two universes.
For each participant i, we define two potential outcomes:

Yi(1) = the outcome we would observe if person i were assigned to the treatment (the violent game). This is the value in Universe 1.
Yi(0) = the outcome we would observe if person i were assigned to the control (the neutral game). This is the value in Universe 0.

For Anna, Y(1) = 6 (her aggression score in the universe where she played the violent game) and Y(0) = 4 (her aggression score in the universe where she played the neutral game).
The individual causal effect for person i is the difference between these two potential outcomes:
\[
\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)
\]
For Anna, \(\tau_{\text{Anna}} = 6 - 4 = 2\). The violent game raised her aggression score by 2 points relative to what it would have been under the neutral game.
The word “potential” is the key word here. Y(1) and Y(0) are quantities that would be observed under each treatment. They are well-defined regardless of which treatment the person actually receives. The treatment Anna actually got determines which of Y(1) and Y(0) we observe; the other one remains a potential outcome that was never realized for her specifically.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
text:
40.3 A small worked example
Consider a tiny study with three participants: Anna, Ben, and Carla. Imagine for a moment that we have x-ray vision and can see both potential outcomes for each person:

Y(1) (violent)
Y(0) (neutral)
Individual effect Y(1) − Y(0)

In this thought experiment:

The violent game increased Anna’s aggression by 2 points.
The violent game had no effect on Ben at all.
The violent game increased Carla’s aggression by 4 points.

Notice that the causal effect varies across people. Anna and Carla react differently to the same intervention. Ben does not react at all. This is realistic; not everyone responds to a treatment in the same way, and the potential outcomes framework explicitly accommodates this. Each person has their own pair of potential outcomes, and the individual effect is computed per person.
If we could see this whole table, causal inference would be trivial. We would just average the individual effects to get the average treatment effect for these three people: (2 + 0 + 4)/3 = +2 points of aggression caused by the violent game on average.
But of course, we cannot see this table. In the actual experiment, each person plays only one of the two games. We see the column corresponding to the game they actually played; the other column is missing.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
section: 40.4 The fundamental problem of causal inference
text:
40.4 The fundamental problem of causal inference
Now imagine the actual experiment. The researcher assigns Anna to play the violent game, Ben to play the neutral game, and Carla to play the violent game. The data we observe look like this:



Person
Played
Y(1) (violent)
Y(0) (neutral)




Anna
violent

neutral

For each person, one of the two potential outcomes is observed (the one corresponding to the game they actually played) and the other is missing (the counterfactual). We see Anna’s Y(1) but not her Y(0). We see Ben’s Y(0) but not his Y(1). We see Carla’s Y(1) but not her Y(0).
This missing-data structure is what Rubin called the fundamental problem of causal inference:

For any individual person, we can observe at most one of their potential outcomes. The other one is forever unobservable.

The word “fundamental” is doing real work here. The problem is not that we have a small sample, or that our measurements are noisy, or that we lacked the budget for a bigger study. With a million participants, we would still see only one of the two potential outcomes per person. The “?”s would multiply, but they would still be there. The problem is structural: it follows from the logic of what a causal claim is. It cannot be solved by collecting more data.








Figure 40.2





The blue cells are what the data show us. The grey cells are what we wish we knew but cannot. The fundamental problem is that exactly half of the cells in this table are missing, by the logic of how causal questions work.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
section: 40.5 From individuals to averages: the ATE
text:
40.5 From individuals to averages: the ATE
We cannot estimate individual causal effects because we cannot observe individual counterfactuals. This is a hard wall, and no amount of data collection or cleverer statistics will get us past it for any specific person.
But we can sometimes estimate averages. Even though we cannot see Anna’s Y(0), we can see Ben’s Y(0). Even though we cannot see Ben’s Y(1), we can see Anna’s and Carla’s. If we average the Y(1) values across the people who actually got the treatment, and we average the Y(0) values across the people who got the control, we might be able to estimate the average difference between the two universes across the population.
This averaged quantity is called the average treatment effect, or ATE:
\[
\text{ATE} = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]
\]
In words: the ATE is the mean of Y(1) across the population minus the mean of Y(0) across the population. Equivalently, it is the average across persons of Y(1) − Y(0).
For our three-person example, where we have x-ray vision:

Mean of Y(1) across Anna, Ben, Carla = (6 + 5 + 7) / 3 = 6
Mean of Y(0) across Anna, Ben, Carla = (4 + 5 + 3) / 3 = 4
ATE = 6 − 4 = +2

The ATE tells us that on average, across this small population, the violent game raises aggression by 2 points. We cannot say which individual gets a 0-point boost (Ben) and which gets a 4-point boost (Carla). But we can say that on average, the boost is 2 points.
For most practical research questions, the ATE is what we want. Drug trials want the average effect of the drug across patients; education research wants the average effect of a curriculum across classrooms; policy research wants the average effect of an intervention across communities. We give up on individual effects (which the fundamental problem makes inaccessible) and aim for the achievable average instead.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
text:
40.6 Why averaging helps
Here is the key insight that makes causal inference possible at all. Even though we cannot see the full column for Y(1) or for Y(0), we might be able to estimate the averages of those columns by using different people for each estimate.
Specifically: if we have one group of people who actually played the violent game, we can use their observed aggression scores to estimate \(E[Y(1)]\). If we have another group of people who actually played the neutral game, we can use their observed scores to estimate \(E[Y(0)]\). The difference between these two group means is a candidate estimate of the ATE.
This is exactly the comparison we have been computing throughout the book. The two-group mean comparison in Chapter 14 (mean as a model), the t-test in Chapter 23, the regression coefficient on condition in Chapter 17, all of these are computing the same quantity: the difference between the mean of Y in the treatment group and the mean of Y in the control group. We will call this quantity the observed group mean difference:
\[
\widehat{\Delta} = \bar{Y}_{\text{treatment group}} - \bar{Y}_{\text{control group}}
\]
The question is whether \(\widehat{\Delta}\), which we can compute from observed data, equals the ATE, which we want to know. The answer is sometimes yes, sometimes no, and the difference between the two is what defines the rest of Section 6.
The key issue is which people end up in the treatment group and which people end up in the control group. If the two groups are exchangeable with respect to potential outcomes (meaning, the average Y(1) among the people in the treatment group is the same as the average Y(1) among the people in the control group, and the same for Y(0)), then \(\widehat{\Delta}\) equals the ATE and we have a clean causal estimate. If the two groups are not exchangeable, then \(\widehat{\Delta}\) mixes the ATE with pre-existing differences between the groups and is not a clean causal estimate.
Exchangeability does not happen by accident. It is purchased by design. The cleanest way to purchase it is random assignment, the topic of Chapter 41. When randomization is not available, we can sometimes purchase exchangeability by careful adjustment for the right covariates, the topic of Chapters 42 to 44.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
section: 40.7 Connection to what you have done already
text:
40.7 Connection to what you have done already
Recall that in Chapter 17 you ran a regression on vgames_study to compare aggression in the violent and neutral conditions. The output included a coefficient of approximately 1.35 with a 95% confidence interval that excluded zero. In the potential outcomes framework, that coefficient is the observed group mean difference \(\widehat{\Delta}\). We computed it on the data we had. The conceptual question is whether \(\widehat{\Delta}\) in vgames_study estimates the ATE of playing the violent game on aggression.
The answer depends entirely on how participants were assigned to conditions. If the assignment was random (as we have implicitly assumed in earlier chapters), then yes: \(\widehat{\Delta}\) estimates the ATE, and the 1.35-point coefficient is a causal estimate. If the assignment was not random, then \(\widehat{\Delta}\) is just the observed group mean difference, and it may or may not equal the ATE depending on how the groups happened to differ at baseline.
This is the conceptual move you should sit with for a moment. The lm() output is the same number either way. The math is the same. What changes is whether that number is the ATE (a causal quantity) or just a descriptive difference (not a causal quantity). The framework for telling these two apart is what the rest of Section 6 will build. Chapter 41 explains why random assignment delivers the ATE for free. Chapters 42 to 44 explain what we can do when random assignment is not available.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
text:
40.8 Summary
The potential outcomes framework gives us:

A formal definition of what it means for X to cause Y in any specific person: the difference between Y(1) and Y(0) for that person.
A formal statement of why causal claims are hard: the fundamental problem of causal inference says we never see both potential outcomes for any individual.
A workable target: the average treatment effect (ATE), the average difference between Y(1) and Y(0) across the population, which can sometimes be estimated from observed group means.
A clear bridge to standard statistical tools: the observed group mean difference (a t-test, a regression coefficient on a treatment dummy) is a candidate estimator of the ATE, and the question of whether it actually estimates the ATE depends on the design of the study.

This framework is more than a thinking aid. It is the language we will use throughout Section 6 to specify exactly what a causal claim is, what it requires, and when we can and cannot make one. Chapter 41 picks up from here and develops randomization as the cleanest path from the observed group mean difference to the ATE.

title: 40  The potential outcomes framework
text:
40.9 Check your understanding
1. What is a potential outcome in the Rubin causal model framework?

 A potential outcome is a future observation that the researcher will collect in a follow-up study, used to validate the causal claims made from the current dataset. A potential outcome is the value of the outcome variable that would be observed under a specific treatment assignment, regardless of whether the person actually received that treatment; each person has one potential outcome per possible treatment level. A potential outcome is an outcome variable that has not yet been measured because the researcher has not yet decided which variables to record, with the choice typically being made after the data have been collected. A potential outcome is the predicted value of the outcome variable from a regression model, used to evaluate model fit and to identify outliers in the residuals.

2. What does the fundamental problem of causal inference state?

 The fundamental problem of causal inference is that researchers often fail to collect enough data to detect causal effects with adequate statistical power. The fundamental problem of causal inference is that for any individual person we can observe at most one of their potential outcomes (the one corresponding to the treatment they actually received), and the other potential outcome is structurally unobservable and cannot be recovered by collecting more data. The fundamental problem of causal inference is that p-values do not directly tell us the probability that a causal hypothesis is true, leaving the substantive causal conclusion uncertain. The fundamental problem of causal inference is that participants in experimental studies often drop out before completing the protocol, leading to missing data that biases the estimated causal effect.

3. What is the average treatment effect (ATE)?

 The average treatment effect (ATE) is the median difference between treated and untreated observations in a sample, used in robust statistical procedures as an alternative to the mean. The average treatment effect (ATE) is the mean of Y(1) - Y(0) across the population, equivalently the mean of Y(1) minus the mean of Y(0); it is a population-level quantity that abandons the goal of estimating individual causal effects in favor of an achievable average. The average treatment effect (ATE) is the standardized effect size (Cohen's d) of the treatment versus control comparison, with the standardization performed using the pooled standard deviation of the two groups. The average treatment effect (ATE) is the predicted value of the outcome variable for a hypothetical participant whose covariates take the average value across the sample, regardless of which treatment they received.

4. What is the relationship between the observed group mean difference and the ATE?

 The observed group mean difference (Y-bar in the treatment group minus Y-bar in the control group) estimates the ATE only when the two groups are exchangeable with respect to potential outcomes; otherwise, the difference mixes the ATE with pre-existing differences between the groups and is not a clean causal estimate. The observed group mean difference (Y-bar in the treatment group minus Y-bar in the control group) always estimates the ATE, regardless of how participants were assigned to conditions, because the linear model used to compute it is by construction unbiased for any underlying causal structure. The observed group mean difference (Y-bar in the treatment group minus Y-bar in the control group) is the same quantity as the individual causal effect for a randomly chosen participant, so it directly informs us about what would happen to any specific person if assigned to the treatment. The observed group mean difference (Y-bar in the treatment group minus Y-bar in the control group) estimates the ATE only when the sample size is sufficiently large to satisfy the central limit theorem, with the threshold typically taken to be 30 participants per group.

5. How does the regression coefficient from lm(aggression ~ condition) in Chapter 17 relate to the potential outcomes framework introduced in this chapter?

 The regression coefficient computed by lm(aggression ~ condition) in Chapter 17 was a different mathematical quantity from the observed group mean difference, because the regression framework explicitly accounts for the causal structure of the data. The regression coefficient computed by lm(aggression ~ condition) in Chapter 17 is mathematically identical to the observed group mean difference, and whether it estimates the average treatment effect depends entirely on the design (how participants were assigned to conditions), not on the statistical procedure used to compute it. The regression coefficient computed by lm(aggression ~ condition) in Chapter 17 was an estimate of the median treatment effect rather than the average treatment effect, with the distinction being important for skewed outcomes such as aggression scores. The regression coefficient computed by lm(aggression ~ condition) in Chapter 17 was estimated under the assumption that the treatment was randomly assigned, and the calculation would have been substantively different had the assignment been non-random.
